rubric.evidence_requirements: Must state compensation point = 75 μmol photons/m²/s (where net O₂ = 0). Must explain that at this point the rate of O₂ produced by photosynthesis equals the rate of O₂ consumed by cellular respiration (gross photosynthesis = respiration), so net gas exchange = 0. Accept: "photosynthesis rate equals respiration rate"; "gross photosynthesis = 2.0 μmol O₂/m²/s to offset the dark respiration rate." Boundary: stating only "net O2 = 0" or "the line crosses zero" identifies the compensation point but does NOT satisfy the explanation requirement; the response must state that the photosynthesis rate equals the cellular respiration rate.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the light compensation point and explain what it indicates about the rates of photosynthesis and respiration.
rubric.minimum_fix: Light compensation point = 75 μmol photons/m²/s; at this intensity photosynthesis rate = cellular respiration rate so net O₂ exchange = 0.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must predict compensation point DECREASES (shifts to lower light intensity / shifts left). Must explain: more CO₂ available → Calvin cycle can fix carbon faster at lower light levels → gross photosynthesis rate rises at any given light intensity → the light intensity at which gross photosynthesis offsets the fixed respiration cost is lower. Accept: "compensation point decreases because Calvin cycle is no longer CO₂-limited, so less light is needed to drive enough photosynthesis to balance respiration."
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain the effect of doubling CO₂ concentration on the light compensation point.
rubric.minimum_fix: Compensation point decreases; more CO₂ increases Calvin cycle rate at each light level so lower light intensity is needed to offset respiration.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include: (1) Light absorbed by P680 (PSII) excites electrons → electrons passed to plastoquinone → cytochrome b6f complex → plastocyanin → P700 (PSI) → ferredoxin → NADP⁺ reductase → NADPH. Accept simplified: electrons flow through ETC. (2) Electron flow through cytochrome b6f pumps H⁺ from stroma into thylakoid lumen, building a proton gradient (low pH in lumen). (3) H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) → drives ATP synthesis (phosphorylation of ADP + Pi). Two of these three elements required for full credit.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how light energy is converted to ATP in the light reactions, including the electron transport chain, proton gradient, and ATP synthase.
rubric.minimum_fix: Light excites electrons → ETC pumps H⁺ into thylakoid lumen → proton gradient drives H⁺ through ATP synthase → ATP synthesized by chemiosmosis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: First stable compound: 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA / PGA). Must state ¹⁴CO₂ is fixed by RuBisCO onto RuBP → unstable 6-carbon intermediate immediately splits → two 3-PGA molecules. RuBP prediction: RuBP concentration DECREASES after light is turned off. Explanation: RuBP is regenerated from G3P using ATP and NADPH (products of light reactions); when light stops, ATP and NADPH are no longer produced → Calvin cycle cannot regenerate RuBP → RuBP is consumed by RuBisCO (CO₂ still present briefly) but not replaced → [RuBP] falls.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the first stable ¹⁴C-labeled compound and predict what happens to RuBP concentration when the light is turned off.
rubric.minimum_fix: ¹⁴C first appears in 3-PGA (3-phosphoglycerate). RuBP concentration decreases after light turns off because ATP and NADPH needed to regenerate RuBP are no longer produced.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must trace: G3P (from Calvin cycle, chloroplast stroma) → exported to cytoplasm → used to synthesize glucose (gluconeogenesis/glycolysis reversal, cytoplasm) → glucose enters glycolysis (cytoplasm) → pyruvate → transported into mitochondrial matrix → acetyl-CoA (via pyruvate dehydrogenase) → Krebs/citric acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix) → NADH/FADH₂ → electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane) → oxidative phosphorylation → ATP. Minimum: G3P → glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → Krebs cycle → electrons to ETC → OXPHOS. Two specific intermediates and correct compartments required.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the molecular pathway linking Calvin cycle products to oxidative phosphorylation, naming intermediates and compartments.
rubric.minimum_fix: G3P (chloroplast) → glucose (cytoplasm, via glycolysis in reverse or sugar synthesis) → pyruvate (cytoplasm via glycolysis) → acetyl-CoA (mitochondrial matrix) → Krebs cycle → NADH/FADH₂ → ETC (inner mitochondrial membrane) → oxidative phosphorylation → ATP.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The light compensation point is the light intensity at which the net rate of gas exchange between a leaf and its environment equals zero.
    (i) Using the data in the table, identify the light compensation point for the spinach leaf disks and explain what it indicates about the relative rates of photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
    (ii) Predict and explain how the light compensation point would change if CO₂ concentration in the experiment were doubled from 0.03% to 0.06%.

(b) Describe the pathway by which energy from light is used to synthesize ATP in the light reactions of photosynthesis. Include the roles of the electron transport chain, the proton gradient, and ATP synthase in your answer.

(c) A student places illuminated spinach leaf disks into a solution containing radioactive ¹⁴CO₂. After 5 minutes of illumination, the light is turned off. Identify the first stable organic compound in which ¹⁴C would appear, and predict what happens to the concentration of RuBP in the chloroplast stroma during the first 2 minutes after the light is turned off. Explain your reasoning.

(d) Describe the specific molecular pathway by which the organic products of the Calvin cycle ultimately provide fuel for oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria, naming at least two intermediate molecules and the cellular compartments in which each step occurs.
items.stimulus:
A student uses the floating leaf disk assay to measure photosynthesis in spinach (Spinacia oleracea). Leaf disks are infiltrated with a sodium bicarbonate solution and placed in a 100 mL beaker illuminated at varying light intensities. The number of floating disks (indicating net O₂ production) is recorded at 10-minute intervals.

Net O₂ exchange (μmol O₂ / m² / s) at different light intensities:

Light intensity (μmol photons/m²/s) | Net O₂ exchange
0 (dark)                            | −2.0
25                                  | −1.2
50                                  | −0.3
75                                  | 0.0
100                                 | +1.4
200                                 | +3.1
400                                 | +4.8
600                                 | +5.0
800                                 | +5.0

All measurements conducted at 25°C, 0.03% CO₂, ambient humidity.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include at least 3 of the following 4 steps with molecular detail: (1) Epinephrine binds β-adrenergic receptor → receptor undergoes conformational change; (2) Active receptor acts as GEF → Gα subunit exchanges GDP for GTP → Gα-GTP dissociates from Gβγ; (3) Gα-GTP activates adenylyl cyclase → adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP; (4) cAMP binds regulatory subunits of PKA → regulatory subunits dissociate → catalytic subunits of PKA become active. Two points: 1 pt for receptor-G protein activation (steps 1-2), 1 pt for cAMP production and PKA activation (steps 3-4).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the molecular events from epinephrine binding to PKA activation, naming key components.
rubric.minimum_fix: Epinephrine binds receptor → receptor activates Gs protein (GDP→GTP exchange on Gα) → Gα-GTP activates adenylyl cyclase → ATP converted to cAMP → cAMP activates PKA (by releasing regulatory subunits from catalytic subunits).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must predict: cAMP levels are PERMANENTLY ELEVATED / constitutively high. Must explain: normally Gs-GTPase hydrolyzes GTP→GDP to terminate signaling; without GTPase activity, Gα-GTP cannot be inactivated → Gα permanently activates adenylyl cyclase → adenylyl cyclase continuously converts ATP to cAMP → cAMP accumulates at high levels. 1 pt for correct prediction + 1 pt for mechanistic explanation referencing GTPase inactivation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain the effect of the GTPase-null Gs mutation on intracellular cAMP levels.
rubric.minimum_fix: cAMP is permanently elevated because the Gs alpha subunit cannot hydrolyze GTP to GDP, so it remains permanently active, continuously activating adenylyl cyclase even without epinephrine.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must predict: constitutive glycogen BREAKDOWN (elevated glucose output) and/or inhibition of glycogen SYNTHESIS. Must explain molecular basis: high cAMP → PKA constitutively active → PKA continuously phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase (activating it, promoting glycogen breakdown) and glycogen synthase (inhibiting it, stopping glycogen synthesis) → net result: glycogen is continuously degraded even in the absence of epinephrine. 1 pt for correct metabolic prediction + 1 pt for connecting to PKA phosphorylation of specific targets.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict the effect on glycogen metabolism in liver cells and explain the molecular basis.
rubric.minimum_fix: Glycogen is constitutively broken down and synthesis is inhibited because PKA (driven by always-high cAMP) permanently phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase while phosphorylating and inactivating glycogen synthase.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must address all 4 dimensions as a comparison (not separate descriptions): (1) Receptor location: epinephrine → cell surface GPCR (water-soluble cannot cross membrane); cortisol → intracellular receptor (cytoplasm or nucleus — lipid-soluble crosses plasma membrane); (2) Signal amplification: epinephrine pathway has multiple amplification steps (one receptor activates many G proteins → many adenylyl cyclase → many cAMP → many PKA → many substrates); cortisol has limited amplification (one hormone → one receptor → modest transcriptional effect); (3) Speed: epinephrine → fast (seconds to minutes, enzyme activation); cortisol → slow (hours, requires new mRNA and protein synthesis); (4) Response type: epinephrine → post-translational modification (phosphorylation of existing proteins); cortisol → changes gene expression (transcription of new genes). Award 1 pt per 2 correct comparative dimensions.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare epinephrine and cortisol signal transduction by receptor location, amplification, speed, and response type.
rubric.minimum_fix: Epinephrine acts at cell surface GPCR (cannot cross membrane) with fast response via enzyme cascades; cortisol crosses the membrane to bind intracellular receptor, acts slowly by regulating gene transcription. Epinephrine has greater signal amplification; cortisol produces longer-lasting changes in gene expression.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must explain that downstream signal transduction components (not just receptors) determine cellular response. Accept any mechanistically sound explanation such as: (1) Different effector proteins expressed — one cell has glycogen phosphorylase (liver) while another has lipase (fat cell) → same cAMP/PKA activation produces different metabolic outputs; (2) Different co-receptors or scaffolding proteins that route the signal differently; (3) Differential expression of phosphatases or PDE that alter signal duration; (4) Different downstream target genes in different cell types. Key concept: cell type-specific response depends on the constellation of signaling and effector proteins present in the cell, not just receptor density.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how two cell types with equal epinephrine receptor numbers can respond differently to the same epinephrine concentration.
rubric.minimum_fix: Even with identical receptor numbers, cells express different downstream signaling proteins and effector molecules — for example, liver cells express glycogen phosphorylase while adipocytes express hormone-sensitive lipase, so the same PKA activation produces glycogen breakdown in liver but triglyceride breakdown in fat cells.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe the molecular events that occur from the binding of epinephrine to its receptor to the activation of protein kinase A (PKA). Include the names and roles of all key molecular components in the pathway.

(b) A researcher discovers a somatic mutation in a patient's tumor cells that permanently abolishes the GTPase activity of the Gs alpha subunit.
    (i) Predict and explain the effect of this mutation on intracellular cAMP levels.
    (ii) Predict the effect of this mutation on glycogen metabolism in liver cells, and explain the molecular basis for your prediction.

(c) Compare and contrast signal transduction by epinephrine (a water-soluble hormone) with signal transduction by cortisol (a lipid-soluble hormone) by addressing: receptor location, signal amplification, speed of response, and type of cellular response. Organize your response as a comparison, not separate descriptions.

(d) Cells often respond differently to the same signal depending on which signal transduction proteins they express. Explain how two different cell types can respond differently to the same concentration of epinephrine, even if both cell types have the same number of epinephrine receptors at their surface.
items.stimulus:
Epinephrine (adrenaline) is a water-soluble hormone released from the adrenal medulla in response to stress. It binds to β-adrenergic receptors, a class of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). The signaling cascade:

1. Epinephrine → β-adrenergic receptor (GPCR)
2. Receptor → activates Gs protein (α subunit exchanges GDP → GTP)
3. Gα-GTP → activates adenylyl cyclase
4. Adenylyl cyclase → converts ATP → cAMP (second messenger)
5. cAMP → activates protein kinase A (PKA)
6. PKA → phosphorylates target proteins

Key downstream effects in liver:
• Glycogen phosphorylase: phosphorylated by PKA → ACTIVATED (breaks down glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate)
• Glycogen synthase: phosphorylated by PKA → INACTIVATED (stops glycogen synthesis)

Signal termination: Gs-GTPase hydrolyzes GTP → GDP (turns off Gα); phosphodiesterase (PDE) degrades cAMP → 5'AMP; protein phosphatases remove phosphate groups from PKA targets.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive. Evidence must include at least 2 of: (1) affected offspring (II-1, II-3) from two unaffected parents is impossible under dominant models → recessive; (2) both sexes affected roughly equally → not X-linked; (3) I-1 is affected but her children include unaffected individuals → if dominant, all children would be affected (unless I-1 is heterozygous) but multiple unaffected children better supports recessive; if X-linked recessive, II-4 (unaffected male) would need to be a carrier which males cannot be. Genotypes: I-1 = aa (affected); I-2 = Aa (unaffected carrier — must have affected children); II-3 = aa (affected); II-4 = Aa (unaffected carrier, given in problem). 1 pt for correct mode with evidence, 1 pt for all four genotypes correct.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Determine mode of inheritance with pedigree evidence; assign genotypes to I-1, I-2, II-3, II-4.
rubric.minimum_fix: Autosomal recessive. Evidence: affected children born to two unaffected parents (I-2 must be carrier); both sexes affected; I-1 (aa) × I-2 (Aa) → II-3 (aa), II-4 (Aa).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Cross: II-3 (aa) × II-4 (Aa). Punnett square: Aa : aa = 1:1. Probability of affected child (aa) = 1/2 = 50%. Must show work via Punnett square or explicit probability statement. Incorrect mode of inheritance from part (a) can earn follow-through credit if correctly applied.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Determine the probability that the first child of II-3 × II-4 will be affected.
rubric.minimum_fix: aa × Aa → 1/2 Aa (carrier, unaffected) : 1/2 aa (affected). Probability = 1/2 or 50%.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Setup: Expected ratio from aa × Aa = 1/2 unaffected : 1/2 affected. Expected from 4 children: 2 unaffected, 2 affected. Observed: 3 unaffected, 1 affected. χ² = (3-2)²/2 + (1-2)²/2 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0. Degrees of freedom = 1, χ²_crit = 3.84. Since χ² calculated (1.0) < χ²_crit (3.84), fail to reject null hypothesis. Conclusion: the data are consistent with the expected 1:1 ratio; the deviation is not statistically significant (likely due to small sample size). 1 pt for correct χ² calculation, 1 pt for correct conclusion with comparison to critical value.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Chi-square analysis of 3 unaffected : 1 affected offspring from 4 children.
rubric.minimum_fix: Expected: 2 unaffected, 2 affected. χ² = (3-2)²/2 + (1-2)²/2 = 1.0. Since 1.0 < 3.84 (critical value), fail to reject null; data are consistent with expected 1:1 ratio.

rubric.evidence_requirements: 8 cM = 8% recombination frequency. In coupling test cross (AB/ab × ab/ab): Parental classes (non-recombinant): AB = (0.92/2)×200 = 92; ab = 92. Recombinant classes: Ab = (0.08/2)×200 = 8; aB = 8. Total = 200. If unlinked (50% recombination): each class = 50 offspring each (1:1:1:1). Linked genes: parental combinations are MORE frequent than expected from independent assortment; recombinant classes are rarer because crossing-over between the loci is required and only occurs in ~8% of meioses. 1 pt for correct four class numbers (92:8:8:92), 1 pt for explanation of why unlinked gives 1:1:1:1.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict offspring classes in a test cross with 8 cM linkage; explain why unlinked genes give 1:1:1:1.
rubric.minimum_fix: Parental classes: ~92 each (AB and ab); Recombinant classes: ~8 each (Ab and aB). Unlinked genes give 1:1:1:1 because independent assortment produces all four gamete types with equal frequency; with linkage, parental combinations are more frequent because recombination is required to generate recombinants.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Meiosis II nondisjunction: after meiosis I has correctly separated homologs, during meiosis II the sister chromatids of ONE chromosome fail to separate. This produces two abnormal gametes from one cell: one gamete with TWO copies of the same chromatid (isodisomy — both copies are identical/from the same original chromatid) and one gamete with NO copy. If the gamete with two copies (n+1 = 2 copies of chr. 7) is fertilized by a normal gamete that contributes 0 copies of chr. 7 (which would require selective loss of the normal chromosome after fertilization — called trisomy rescue), the result is uniparental isodisomy: child has two copies of chromosome 7 from the same parent. OR: meiosis II nondisjunction → n+1 gamete → fertilized by n gamete → trisomic → trisomy rescue eliminates one copy → if the remaining two copies are both from the same parent, uniparental isodisomy results. 1 pt for correctly identifying stage (meiosis II, after proper meiosis I) and mechanism; 1 pt for describing the resulting gamete type (n+1, two identical chromatids) and how it produces isodisomy.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how meiosis II nondisjunction produces uniparental isodisomy.
rubric.minimum_fix: Nondisjunction in meiosis II produces a gamete with two identical copies of one chromosome (from failure of sister chromatid separation). If that gamete is fertilized and the extra chromosome from the other parent is subsequently lost (trisomy rescue), the child retains two copies of the chromosome from the same parent = uniparental isodisomy.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the pedigree, determine the most likely mode of inheritance of Syndrome X (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, or X-linked recessive). Provide evidence from the pedigree to justify your answer. Then determine the genotypes of individuals I-1, I-2, II-3, and II-4.

(b) Individual II-3 and individual II-4 (who is phenotypically unaffected but a known carrier) plan to have children.
    (i) Using a Punnett square or probability notation, determine the probability that their first child will be affected by Syndrome X.
    (ii) Individual II-3 and II-4 have four children. Three are unaffected and one is affected. Perform a chi-square (χ²) analysis to determine whether these data are consistent with the expected ratio. Use a significance level of p = 0.05 and 1 degree of freedom (χ²_crit = 3.84).

(c) A new genetic test reveals that the gene responsible for Syndrome X is located on chromosome 7, approximately 8 cM from a molecular marker called M1. In a test cross of an individual heterozygous at both loci (in coupling) with a doubly homozygous recessive individual, 200 offspring are produced.
    (i) Predict the number of offspring expected in each of the four phenotypic classes.
    (ii) Explain why the actual offspring frequencies would differ from a 1:1:1:1 ratio if these genes were unlinked.

(d) Explain how nondisjunction during meiosis II in one parent could produce a child with two copies of the chromosome 7 allele from that parent (uniparental isodisomy). Describe at what stage nondisjunction would have to occur and what type of gamete would result.
items.stimulus:
Pedigree for Syndrome X (three generations):

Generation I:  I-1 (affected female) × I-2 (unaffected male)
Generation II: II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected female), II-3 (affected female), II-4 (unaffected male), II-5 (unaffected male), II-6 (unaffected female)
Generation III: III-1 (unaffected), III-2 (affected), III-3 (unaffected), III-4 (unaffected)

Note: II-3 and II-4 are mated (III-1 through III-4 are their children). II-4 is a known carrier.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include: (1) Design — bacteria grown in heavy ¹⁵N medium → DNA becomes all-heavy; then switched to ¹⁴N medium → allow one or two rounds of replication; DNA isolated and centrifuged in CsCl gradient to separate by density; (2) Results — after 1st replication: ONE BAND at intermediate density (hybrid ¹⁵N/¹⁴N); after 2nd replication: TWO BANDS — one intermediate, one light; (3) Interpretation — semiconservative predicts hybrid at generation 1 (one old ¹⁵N strand + one new ¹⁴N strand per molecule); dispersive predicts one intermediate band at generation 1 too, but generation 2 dispersive predicts ONE band (still intermediate) vs. semiconservative (two bands). Conservative predicts one heavy + one light band after generation 1 (not seen). The two-band result at generation 2 eliminates dispersive and confirms semiconservative. 1 pt for design/results, 1 pt for eliminating at least one alternative model with explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the Meselson-Stahl experiment and explain how results support semiconservative replication.
rubric.minimum_fix: Bacteria grown in ¹⁵N → switched to ¹⁴N → DNA banded in CsCl gradient; after generation 1: one hybrid band; after generation 2: hybrid + light bands. This eliminates conservative (would give heavy + light at gen 1) and dispersive (would give one gradually lightening band at gen 2) models.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must correctly describe each role: (1) Helicase — unwinds/unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs; creates the replication fork; (2) DNA primase — synthesizes short RNA primers complementary to the template strand; provides the 3'-OH that DNA polymerase requires to begin synthesis (DNA polymerase cannot initiate de novo); (3) DNA polymerase III — synthesizes the new DNA strand by adding deoxyribonucleotides to the 3'-OH of the primer, reading the template 3'→5' and synthesizing 5'→3'; proofreads via 3'→5' exonuclease; (4) DNA ligase — joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent DNA fragments after RNA primers are removed and replaced. Award 1 pt per 2 correct enzyme descriptions (minimum: role must be mechanistically correct).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the roles of helicase, DNA primase, DNA polymerase III, and DNA ligase in replication.
rubric.minimum_fix: Helicase unwinds DNA; primase makes RNA primers so polymerase can start; DNA pol III synthesizes new strand 5'→3' using template; ligase joins Okazaki fragments on lagging strand.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Write the mRNA sequence; determine the amino acid sequence; analyze the point mutation.
rubric.minimum_fix: mRNA transcribed from template 5'-ATCGGATCCAAGTCG-3' (read 3'→5' by RNA pol) is 5'-CGACUUGGAUCCGAU-3'. Codons: CGA-CUU-GGA-UCC-GAU = Arg-Leu-Gly-Ser-Asp (no AUG start or UAA/UAG/UGA stop in this segment). Mutation at position 6 (A→change in template): evaluate synonymous vs nonsynonymous based on whether amino acid changes. Point mutation: synonymous if new codon encodes same amino acid; nonsynonymous if amino acid changes → altered protein structure/function possible.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must explain mechanism first: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are the enzymes that attach the correct amino acid to the correct tRNA (charging the tRNA). Each synthetase is specific for one amino acid and recognizes the corresponding tRNA anticodon. Blocking them → tRNAs cannot be charged with amino acids → uncharged tRNAs accumulate; tRNA cannot deliver amino acids to the ribosome → translation halts (ribosomes stall at the A site, waiting for aminoacyl-tRNA) → no new proteins are synthesized → cell loses ability to make all proteins → cell dies. Additional consequences: accumulation of uncharged tRNAs; ribosome stalling; activation of amino acid starvation response (stringent response in bacteria); in eukaryotes, activation of integrated stress response (ISR), eIF2α phosphorylation. 1 pt for mechanism (tRNA not charged, translation halted), 1 pt for cellular consequence (all protein synthesis stops → cell death / stress response).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain the consequences of blocking aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
rubric.minimum_fix: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs with their correct amino acids. Blocking them → tRNAs remain uncharged → cannot deliver amino acids to ribosomes → translation halts globally → all protein synthesis stops → cell cannot maintain homeostasis → cell death.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The Meselson-Stahl experiment demonstrated that DNA replication is semiconservative. Describe the experimental design and results of the Meselson-Stahl experiment. Explain how the results support the semiconservative model rather than the conservative or dispersive models.

(b) Describe the roles of the following enzymes during DNA replication in eukaryotes, and explain why each is necessary:
    (i) Helicase
    (ii) DNA primase
    (iii) DNA polymerase III (or the equivalent leading-strand polymerase)
    (iv) DNA ligase

(c) The template DNA strand for a gene has the following sequence:
    5'-ATCGGATCCAAGTCG-3'
    (i) Write the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this template strand.
    (ii) Using the genetic code table, determine the amino acid sequence encoded by the mRNA, beginning from the first codon. Identify which codon, if any, is a start codon or stop codon.
    (iii) A point mutation changes the 6th base of the template strand from C to T. Determine whether this mutation is synonymous or nonsynonymous, and explain the consequence for the protein.

(d) A researcher treats cells with a drug that specifically blocks the activity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Predict and explain the cellular consequences of this drug treatment for protein synthesis.
items.stimulus:
DNA replication and gene expression are fundamental processes of the central dogma. Key facts:

• DNA replication is semiconservative: each daughter molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand
• Replication occurs 5'→3' on the new strand; the template is read 3'→5'
• RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA using the template (antisense) strand
• The genetic code is read in triplet codons (non-overlapping)
• AUG = start codon (Met); UAA, UAG, UGA = stop codons

Partial codon table (relevant to part c):
AUC = Ile | GGA = Gly | UCC = Ser | AAG = Lys | UCG = Ser
AUG = Met | CCA = Pro | AGU = Ser | CUU = Leu
UAG = stop | UCA = Ser | GAC = Asp | GUC = Val

rubric.evidence_requirements: Condition 1 (glucose+, lactose-): Very low. Repressor is active (no allolactose to inactivate it) → operator blocked. CAP inactive (glucose present → low cAMP). BOTH negative control ON and positive control OFF → lowest expression. Condition 2 (glucose+, lactose+): Low. Repressor inactivated by allolactose → operator free. BUT CAP inactive (glucose → low cAMP) → RNA pol binds weakly. Negative control off, positive control off → basal transcription only. Condition 3 (glucose-, lactose-): Very low. No allolactose → repressor active → blocks operator. Even though cAMP high and CAP active (positive control ON), repressor blocks access → negligible transcription. Condition 4 (glucose-, lactose+): Very high. Allolactose inactivates repressor (negative control OFF) AND no glucose → high cAMP → CAP-cAMP binds upstream site → strongly enhances RNAP binding (positive control ON). Both regulatory mechanisms favor transcription → maximum expression. Award 1 pt for correctly explaining Conditions 1 and 4 with molecular detail; 1 pt for 2 and 3.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain lacZ expression under all four conditions using lac repressor, allolactose, CAP, and cAMP.
rubric.minimum_fix: Cond 1: Low — repressor blocks operator (no allolactose) AND CAP inactive (glucose present). Cond 2: Low — repressor off (allolactose), but CAP still inactive. Cond 3: Low — repressor on (no allolactose), even with CAP active. Cond 4: High — repressor off AND CAP active: both controls favor transcription.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Operator mutant cannot bind repressor: Condition 1: NOW HIGH — repressor cannot block operator even though active → transcription occurs; CAP still inactive but basal promoter activity still allowed; expect medium-high. Condition 2: High (similar reasoning, repressor irrelevant). Condition 3: Medium — CAP active (no glucose, high cAMP) → some enhancement, repressor cannot block; expression depends on CAP alone. Condition 4: Very high — same as WT condition 4, since repressor was already inactive in WT condition 4; CAP still active. Summary: in all conditions where glucose is absent lacZ is highly expressed; in glucose conditions, lacZ is expressed at basal levels (no repressor blocking, but CAP inactive). Trans vs. cis: this is a CIS-ACTING mutation. The operator is a DNA binding site on the same DNA molecule as the genes it regulates. A mutation in the operator only affects expression of genes on the SAME DNA molecule (same chromosome/plasmid). It cannot be complemented by a wild-type operator on another DNA molecule. Contrast with trans-acting: protein products (like the repressor) can diffuse through the cytoplasm and regulate genes on other DNA molecules. 1 pt for correct predictions with reasoning; 1 pt for correctly identifying cis-acting with explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict lacZ expression for operator-mutant strain; classify mutation as cis or trans.
rubric.minimum_fix: Operator mutant: lacZ constitutively expressed in all conditions (repressor can never bind). This is cis-acting: the operator DNA sequence only affects genes on the same DNA molecule and cannot be complemented by a wild-type operator on another molecule.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Any 3 of the following differences with functional significance: (1) Nuclear compartmentalization — eukaryotes separate transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm), enabling mRNA processing, export checkpoints, and additional regulation layers; prokaryotes couple transcription-translation simultaneously. (2) mRNA processing — eukaryotes have 5' cap, 3' poly-A tail, intron splicing (pre-mRNA → mature mRNA); prokaryotes translate mRNA directly without processing. Alternative splicing in eukaryotes allows one gene to produce multiple protein isoforms. (3) Chromatin structure — eukaryotic DNA is packaged in nucleosomes; accessibility is regulated by histone modifications (acetylation = open; deacetylation = closed); prokaryotes lack histones. (4) Enhancers and silencers — eukaryotic enhancers can be thousands of bp away from the promoter and act by looping to contact the promoter; prokaryotic regulatory sequences are close to the promoter. (5) Multiple transcription factors — eukaryotes use combinatorial TF binding (many TFs interact with mediator complex and general TF machinery); prokaryotes use simpler repressor/activator-promoter interactions. (6) Polycistronic vs. monocistronic — prokaryotic operons encode multiple proteins in one mRNA; eukaryotic mRNAs are usually monocistronic. 1 pt per complete difference with functional significance; max 2 pts (so need at least 2 to score 2/2).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe three structural or mechanistic differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic gene regulation with functional significance.
rubric.minimum_fix: Three examples: (1) Eukaryotes have nuclear compartment — mRNA must be processed and exported before translation, enabling checkpoint regulation not possible in prokaryotes. (2) Enhancers in eukaryotes can be far from the gene and loop to promoter — allows cell-type-specific regulation; prokaryotic control elements are adjacent to genes. (3) Chromatin packaging — eukaryotic nucleosomes must be remodeled for transcription; this is a regulatory layer absent in prokaryotes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: The most likely mechanism is ALTERNATIVE SPLICING. Same genomic DNA (identical pre-mRNA sequence) → different splicing patterns in different cell types → different exon combinations included in mature mRNA → different mRNA sequences despite same DNA. Cell-type-specific splicing factors (SR proteins, hnRNPs) are expressed differently in liver vs. pancreatic cells; these factors bind specific exonic/intronic splicing enhancers or silencers and direct the spliceosome to include or skip specific exons. Other acceptable mechanisms: (1) Alternative transcription start sites (different promoters used in different cell types, producing mRNAs with different 5' sequences); (2) Alternative polyadenylation sites (different 3' ends); (3) RNA editing (A→I or C→U editing, though less common and more tissue-specific). Must name the molecular process and describe the molecular players. 1 pt for identifying the mechanism, 1 pt for explaining the molecular basis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Propose a mechanism to explain identical DNA producing different mRNA sequences in liver vs. pancreatic cells.
rubric.minimum_fix: Alternative splicing: the same pre-mRNA is processed differently in liver vs. pancreatic cells because cell-type-specific splicing regulatory proteins (splicing factors) are differentially expressed, directing the spliceosome to include different exons → different mature mRNA sequences from the same gene.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The experimental results show different levels of lacZ expression under four conditions (see table in stimulus). For each condition, predict the level of lac operon transcription (high, low, or none) based on the state of the regulatory components, and explain your reasoning by describing the roles of the lac repressor, allolactose, CAP, and cAMP.

(b) A mutation in the lac operon operator sequence prevents the lac repressor from binding. Predict the lacZ expression level for this mutant strain under each of the four conditions, and explain whether this mutation is cis-acting or trans-acting.

(c) Eukaryotic gene regulation differs from prokaryotic regulation in several important ways. Using the lac operon as the prokaryotic example and a eukaryotic gene regulated by enhancers and transcription factors as the eukaryotic example, describe THREE specific structural or mechanistic differences in how gene expression is regulated. Do not simply restate definitions — explain the functional significance of each difference.

(d) A researcher performs RNA-seq on the same gene in liver cells and pancreatic cells and finds that the mRNA sequences differ between the two cell types even though the genomic DNA sequence is identical. Propose a mechanism that could explain this result and describe the molecular process responsible.
items.stimulus:
Experimental conditions and lacZ (β-galactosidase) expression levels in wild-type E. coli:

Condition | Glucose | Lactose | Relative lacZ expression
    1     |  +      |   -     | Very low (< 1%)
    2     |  +      |   +     | Low (~5%)
    3     |  -      |   -     | Very low (< 1%)
    4     |  -      |   +     | Very high (100%)

Notes: Glucose presence inhibits adenylyl cyclase → low cAMP → CAP inactive. Lactose is converted to allolactose in the cell, which inactivates the lac repressor. In the absence of glucose, cAMP is high → CAP-cAMP complex binds CAP site upstream of promoter → enhances RNA polymerase binding.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Data analysis: mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976) to 10.07 mm (1978), a shift of ~0.65 mm. This is directional selection toward deeper beaks. Four components: (1) Variation — natural heritable variation in beak depth existed in the 1976 population (beak depth is a heritable polygenic trait with continuous variation); (2) Selective agent — the 1977 drought depleted small soft seeds, leaving only large hard seeds available; birds with larger/deeper beaks had a survival advantage because they could crack large hard seeds; (3) Differential survival — only 85/642 birds survived (13%); survivors had significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population (9.42 mm) — evidence that large beaks conferred survival advantage; (4) Heritability — beak depth is heritable (genetic basis); surviving birds passed their deeper-beak alleles to offspring → 1978 post-drought population showed larger mean beak depth than 1976. Award 1 pt for correct data description (direction and evidence) + 1 pt for addressing at least 3 of the 4 evolutionary mechanism components.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Analyze beak depth data and explain the mechanism of natural selection — variation, selective agent, differential survival, heritability.
rubric.minimum_fix: Beak depth increased ~0.65mm from 1976 to 1978 due to directional selection: drought eliminated small seeds → only birds with deep beaks could crack large seeds → differential survival (only 13% survived, with larger mean beak depth) → heritable deep-beak alleles passed to offspring → population mean shifted.

rubric.evidence_requirements: p = 0.6 (freq D), q = 0.4 (freq d). p + q = 1.0 ✓. Expected H-W genotype frequencies: p² = (0.6)² = 0.36 (DD); 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48 (Dd); q² = (0.4)² = 0.16 (dd). Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. Comparison: DD observed (0.40) > expected (0.36); Dd observed (0.42) < expected (0.48); dd observed (0.18) > expected (0.16). Deviations are present. To formally test, χ²: (0.40-0.36)²/0.36 + (0.42-0.48)²/0.48 + (0.18-0.16)²/0.16 = 0.0044/0.36 + 0.0036/0.48 + 0.0004/0.16 = 0.012 + 0.0075 + 0.0025 = 0.022. With df=1 (for 2-allele), critical value ~3.84. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 → fail to reject H-W equilibrium (deviations not significant). Conclusion: population is approximately in H-W equilibrium. 1 pt for correct expected frequencies; 1 pt for comparison to observed and correct conclusion.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using 1976 allele frequencies; show all calculations.
rubric.minimum_fix: Expected: DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16. Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 critical value → population does not significantly deviate from H-W equilibrium.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) After El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant → small beaks efficient for small soft seeds → directional selection toward SMALLER beaks (opposite direction from drought). OR: if both small and large seeds abundant → stabilizing selection on intermediate beak depth. Most defensible: directional selection toward smaller beaks because small seeds are now abundant and favored. Small-beaked birds can efficiently process abundant small seeds; large seeds may now be scarce; smaller beaks may require less energy to maintain. (ii) Not Lamarckian because: Lamarckian inheritance requires that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime are directly inherited by offspring (use/disuse + inheritance of acquired characteristics). In this case: birds did not develop smaller beaks during their lifetime because seeds got smaller. Rather, birds with pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth (small beaks) happened to have higher fitness in the new environment → differential reproduction → their alleles increased in frequency. The beak size change in the population is due to differential reproduction of pre-existing variants, not inheritance of acquired traits. 1 pt per sub-part.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify selection type after 1983 El Niño; explain why this is not Lamarckian.
rubric.minimum_fix: (i) Directional selection toward smaller beaks — El Niño brought small soft seeds, which small-beaked birds can exploit more efficiently. (ii) Not Lamarckian — birds did not shrink their own beaks in response to environment; rather, small-beaked individuals already in the population survived and reproduced more, passing their heritable alleles forward.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Competitive exclusion principle: two species with identical ecological niches (same resource requirements) cannot coexist indefinitely; the superior competitor will exclude the inferior. G. magnirostris is larger with a deeper beak — better competitor for large hard seeds. If medium ground finch and G. magnirostris compete for the same large hard seeds: G. magnirostris may outcompete and exclude G. fortis → G. fortis population declines or goes locally extinct on Daphne Major. Evolutionary coexistence outcome (any ONE of): (1) Character displacement — natural selection favors G. fortis individuals with beaks different from G. magnirostris (e.g., smaller beaks focusing on small seeds that G. magnirostris cannot exploit efficiently) → two species diverge in beak size → resource partitioning → coexistence; (2) Niche differentiation — G. fortis specializes on different food resources (different seed types, different microhabitat); (3) Temporal partitioning — foraging at different times. Character displacement is the best-supported evolutionary mechanism. Note: actual documentation of character displacement in Galápagos finches is a classic case study. 1 pt for competitive exclusion definition + prediction; 1 pt for evolutionary coexistence mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain competitive exclusion; predict outcome for medium ground finch; describe an evolutionary coexistence outcome.
rubric.minimum_fix: Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist — G. magnirostris would outcompete G. fortis for large seeds → G. fortis may be excluded. Evolutionary coexistence: character displacement — selection favors G. fortis individuals with smaller beaks that exploit small seeds G. magnirostris cannot efficiently use → niche differentiation → stable coexistence.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Analyze the beak depth data from Table 1. Using evidence from the data, describe the change in the finch population's beak depth between 1976 and 1978, and explain the mechanism of natural selection responsible for this change. Address: the source of variation, the selective agent, differential survival, and heritability.

(b) Using the allele frequencies provided in Table 2, determine whether the medium ground finch population in 1976 was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the beak depth gene. Show all calculations. (Use p = frequency of allele D; q = frequency of allele d.)

(c) A 1983 El Niño event brought heavy rainfall to the Galápagos, dramatically increasing the abundance of small soft seeds. By 1984, mean beak depth had shifted back toward smaller values.
    (i) Identify the type of natural selection acting on beak depth after the 1983 El Niño, and explain why small beak depth was favored.
    (ii) Explain why this shift in beak depth does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance.

(d) The large ground finch (Geospiza magnirostris) arrived on Daphne Major Island after 1982 and occupies a similar ecological niche to the medium ground finch. Explain the concept of competitive exclusion and predict what might happen to the medium ground finch population as a result of G. magnirostris's arrival. Describe ONE possible evolutionary outcome for the medium ground finch population that would allow coexistence.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: Mean beak depth (mm) of the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major Island, Galápagos

Year | Mean beak depth (mm) | Sample size | Notes
1976 |        9.42          |    642      | Pre-drought
1977 |        9.96          |    85       | During drought (severe dry season)
1978 |       10.07          |    388      | Post-drought recovery

Drought conditions (1976-1977): Small soft seeds became scarce first; large hard seeds remained available longer. Birds with larger, deeper beaks could crack large seeds that smaller-beaked birds could not process.

Survival: 85 of 642 birds survived the drought. Mean beak depth of survivors = 9.96 mm (significantly larger than pre-drought mean of 9.42 mm).

Table 2: Allele frequencies for a beak depth quantitative trait locus (simplified diploid model)
Allele D (associated with deeper beaks): frequency = 0.6
Allele d (associated with shallower beaks): frequency = 0.4

Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 population (N=642):
DD: 0.40 | Dd: 0.42 | dd: 0.18

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) r = b - d = 0.28 - 0.11 = 0.17 per year. Exponential growth: N(t) = N₀ × e^(rt). N(3) = 980 × e^(0.17×3) = 980 × e^(0.51) = 980 × 1.665 = ~1,632 birds. Alternatively, using discrete: N(t) = N₀(1+r)^t = 980(1.17)³ = 980 × 1.602 = ~1,570 birds. Accept either method with correct setup. (ii) Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources, no competition, no predation, no disease — conditions that do not persist in nature. As population grows, resources (food, space, nesting sites) become limiting → per capita birth rate falls and/or per capita death rate rises → growth rate decelerates → population approaches carrying capacity. 1 pt for correct r calculation and population estimate with work shown; 1 pt for biological explanation of why exponential growth is unsustainable.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate r and predict population after 3 years; explain why exponential growth cannot continue.
rubric.minimum_fix: r = 0.17/year. N(3) ≈ 1,570–1,632 (accept range from discrete or continuous exponential). Exponential growth unsustainable because resources are finite; as population grows, food, space, and other resources become limiting, increasing death rate and/or decreasing birth rate.

rubric.evidence_requirements: K ≈ 1,200 birds. Evidence: from 1982 onward, the population stabilizes around 1,180–1,210 with no consistent upward or downward trend; it oscillates slightly around this value. This plateau is characteristic of a population at carrying capacity. Growth rate behavior approaching K: as N increases toward K, the logistic term (K-N)/K decreases toward 0 → dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K → growth rate falls. Maximum growth rate occurs at N = K/2 = ~600 birds (around 1974–1976 in the data). Growth rate approaches zero as population reaches K. Students may also describe: oscillation around K (overshoot and undershoot), which reflects real-world dynamics. 1 pt for K identification with evidence from table; 1 pt for correct description of decreasing growth rate as population approaches K.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the carrying capacity from the data; describe population growth rate behavior as population approaches K.
rubric.minimum_fix: K ≈ 1,200 birds (population stabilizes 1982–1990 around this value, no sustained increase). As population approaches K, growth rate (dN/dt) decreases toward zero because (K-N)/K → 0; maximum growth rate was at N=K/2≈600.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Drought classification: DENSITY-INDEPENDENT. Justification: a drought reduces seed availability equally regardless of finch population size — it would kill the same proportion of birds whether there were 100 or 10,000. The effect is driven by climate (abiotic), not by the number of finches. Density-dependent explanations: (i) Food competition — as population size increases, more birds compete for the same seed resources → per capita food availability decreases → more birds starve or have reduced reproductive success → death rate rises or birth rate falls in proportion to population density. At low density, food is plentiful per bird; at high density, food is scarce per bird. (ii) Disease transmission — as population density increases, birds come into closer contact → pathogens spread more easily between individuals → transmission rate increases with density (follows mass-action kinetics: transmission ∝ density of susceptible × density of infected) → higher proportion of birds become infected at high density than at low density. 1 pt for density-independent classification with reasoning; 1 pt for both density-dependent mechanisms.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify drought as density-dependent or density-independent; explain food competition and disease as density-dependent.
rubric.minimum_fix: Drought = density-independent (abiotic factor that kills regardless of population density). Food competition is density-dependent: more birds → less food per bird → starvation increases with density. Disease is density-dependent: more birds → easier pathogen transmission → infection rate scales with density.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete experiment design: Hypothesis: Food availability, not predation, is the primary factor limiting K of G. fortis on Daphne Major (or reverse). Independent variable: food availability and/or predator presence (two factors to test). Dependent variable: finch population size / carrying capacity reached. Control group: unmanipulated island plots where food and predators are at natural levels. Experimental groups: Group 1 — food supplementation (add seed at regular intervals) while predators remain at natural levels; Group 2 — predator exclusion (wire enclosures excluding hawks/owls) with food at natural levels; Group 3 (optional) — food supplementation AND predator exclusion. Confounding variables: any 1 example. E.g., seasonal variation in seed production — control by running experiment across multiple seasons and using statistical controls; or habitat area differences between plots — control by using plots of equal area; or immigration/emigration — control by using enclosed populations or mark-recapture. Prediction consistent with hypothesis: if food is primary limit, K will be higher in Group 1 (food-supplemented) than control, but not in Group 2 (predator-excluded); if predation is primary limit, opposite pattern. Award 1 pt for complete experimental design (hypothesis, IV, DV, control, treatment); 1 pt for specific confounding variable with control method.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Design a controlled experiment to distinguish food availability from predation as the primary limiting factor.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypothesis: food availability is the primary limiting factor. IV: food supplementation vs. predator exclusion (experimental groups). DV: population size/carrying capacity. Control: unmanipulated plots. Experimental groups: (1) food added, natural predators; (2) predators excluded, natural food. Confound example: seasonal variation in seeds — control by running experiment across multiple complete years.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) In 1975, a survey of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major found 980 birds. The population had an annual birth rate (b) of 0.28 and an annual death rate (d) of 0.11.
    (i) Calculate the population's intrinsic rate of increase (r) and predict the population size after 3 years, assuming exponential growth. Show all work.
    (ii) Explain why exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely in a natural population.

(b) Table 1 shows finch population data from 1970–1990. Identify the approximate carrying capacity (K) of the Daphne Major finch population from the data, and explain the evidence you used to determine K. Describe what is happening to population growth rate as the population approaches K.

(c) In 1977, a drought reduced the finch population from approximately 1,200 to 85 individuals. Classify this event as a density-dependent or density-independent limiting factor, and justify your classification. Then explain how each of the following factors would limit the finch population in a DENSITY-DEPENDENT manner as the population grows: (i) food competition, (ii) disease transmission.

(d) Design a controlled experiment to determine whether food availability or predation is the primary limiting factor controlling the carrying capacity of the medium ground finch population on Daphne Major. Include: the hypothesis, independent variable, dependent variable, control group, experimental group(s), and at least one potential confounding variable and how you would control for it.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: Geospiza fortis population size on Daphne Major Island (1970–1990)

Year | Population Size
1970 |      300
1972 |      480
1974 |      750
1976 |      980
1977 |       85  (severe drought)
1978 |      380
1980 |      820
1982 |     1,180
1984 |     1,210
1986 |     1,195
1988 |     1,200
1990 |     1,205

Daphne Major is a small volcanic island (~0.34 km²) with limited food resources. Primary food sources: small and large seeds. Predators include: Galápagos hawk (rare), short-eared owl (occasional).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Osmotic equilibrium: approximately 0.35–0.40 M sucrose (between 0.3 M where mass is nearly unchanged at +0.2% and 0.4 M where mass is slightly decreased at −0.2%). Interpolating: equilibrium is at approximately 0.35 M, where mass change = 0%. This concentration equals the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue — at this concentration, the water potential of the solution equals the water potential of the potato, so no net water movement. At 0.2 M sucrose: the solution is LESS concentrated than potato tissue (~0.35 M) → potato tissue has more negative water potential than the solution → water moves INTO the cells by osmosis. Potato cells gain water → cells become turgid (cell wall provides counter-pressure, preventing lysis). 1 pt for identifying equilibrium concentration with reasoning; 1 pt for correct direction of water movement at 0.2 M with explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify osmotic equilibrium concentration; explain water movement direction and cell state at 0.2 M.
rubric.minimum_fix: Equilibrium ≈ 0.35 M (where % mass change = 0). Potato tissue solute concentration ≈ 0.35 M. At 0.2 M: solution is hypotonic to potato → water moves INTO cells → cells become turgid/swell.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Water potential (Ψ): the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water; determines direction of water movement (water moves from high Ψ to low Ψ). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Ψs (solute potential / osmotic potential): always ≤ 0 in solutions; becomes more negative as solute concentration increases; reflects the reduction in water potential due to dissolved solutes. Ψp (pressure potential / turgor pressure): can be positive (pressure from cell wall pushing back) or negative (tension in xylem); reflects the effect of physical pressure on water potential. (ii) At equilibrium with pure water (Ψwater = 0): Ψcell = 0. Ψ = Ψs + Ψp → 0 = −7.0 + Ψp → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This represents full turgor pressure — the cell wall is pushing back with +7.0 bars of pressure against the inward osmotic flow. The cell is fully turgid. 1 pt for correct definitions with equation; 1 pt for correct calculation and interpretation of Ψp = +7.0 bars as turgor pressure.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Define water potential and its components; calculate pressure potential at equilibrium in pure water.
rubric.minimum_fix: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; Ψs = solute potential (negative, due to solutes lowering water potential); Ψp = pressure potential (positive turgor or negative tension). At equilibrium: 0 = −7.0 + Ψp → Ψp = +7.0 bars = full turgor pressure (cell wall resisting inward water flow).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Hypotonic solution (lower solute than cell): Plant cell — water enters by osmosis → cell swells against the rigid cell wall → cell becomes turgid (firm); cell wall prevents bursting; this is the normal, healthy state for plant cells providing structural support. Animal cell (RBC) — water enters by osmosis → cell swells → if sufficiently hypotonic, cell may burst (lyse/cytolysis) because no cell wall provides resistance; RBCs lyse in pure water. (ii) Hypertonic solution (higher solute than cell): Plant cell — water leaves the cell by osmosis → cytoplasm shrinks → cell membrane pulls away from cell wall → plasmolysis; vacuole shrinks; plant wilts; if severe, cell dies. Animal cell (RBC) — water leaves by osmosis → cell shrinks → crenation (cell becomes spiky/star-shaped as membrane buckles). Key difference: plant cells have a cell wall that prevents lysis in hypotonic conditions; animal cells lack a cell wall and can lyse. 1 pt per correct comparison (hypotonic and hypertonic, with plant vs. animal distinction and correct terminology).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare plant cell and animal cell responses in hypotonic and hypertonic solutions.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypotonic: plant cell becomes turgid (cell wall prevents lysis); animal cell (RBC) swells and may lyse. Hypertonic: plant cell undergoes plasmolysis (membrane pulls away from wall); animal cell undergoes crenation (shrinkage/spiky shape).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Aquaporins facilitate osmosis by providing a hydrophilic channel for water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer rapidly and selectively. They do not provide energy or actively pump water — they only lower the activation energy barrier for water movement through the membrane by creating a pore lined with hydrophilic amino acids through which water molecules pass in single file via hydrogen bonding. Water movement through aquaporins is still driven entirely by the water potential gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) — the thermodynamic driving force is unchanged; only the rate (permeability) is increased. This is facilitated diffusion, not active transport. (ii) In hypertonic solution: normal cell — aquaporins allow rapid net efflux of water → cell rapidly loses water → plasmolysis occurs quickly. Aquaporin-deleted cell — water can still cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion (lipid bilayer has some intrinsic water permeability), but much more slowly → plasmolysis occurs more slowly (or is attenuated in rate) but the eventual equilibrium state is the same (still loses water to hypertonic solution). The final equilibrium is driven by thermodynamics, not kinetics — aquaporins affect RATE of water loss, not direction or final equilibrium. 1 pt for correct passive mechanism explanation; 1 pt for predicting slower (not absent) water loss with correct reasoning.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how aquaporins facilitate osmosis without violating passive transport; predict effect of aquaporin deletion in hypertonic solution.
rubric.minimum_fix: Aquaporins provide hydrophilic pores for facilitated diffusion of water — they increase the rate of osmosis without changing its direction or thermodynamic driving force (water still moves from high to low Ψ; no energy input required). Aquaporin-deleted cell in hypertonic solution: loses water more slowly than normal cell (simple diffusion through bilayer is slower than facilitated transport), but eventually reaches same equilibrium state — same final plasmolysis, just slower.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) A student sets up the following experiment: potato (Solanum tuberosum) cylinders of equal mass are placed in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations for 24 hours. Mass change is recorded.
    (i) Using the data in Table 1, graph the percent mass change versus sucrose concentration (or describe the shape of the graph and label key points).
    (ii) Identify the sucrose concentration at which the potato tissue is in osmotic equilibrium with the surrounding solution. Explain what this concentration tells you about the solute concentration of the potato tissue.
    (iii) At the 0.2 M sucrose solution, predict and explain the direction of net water movement and the expected physical state of the potato cells.

(b) Water potential (Ψ) determines the direction of water movement. The water potential of the potato tissue in part (a) is −7.0 bars.
    (i) Define water potential and write the equation: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, defining each term.
    (ii) If the solute potential (Ψs) of the potato tissue is −7.0 bars and the potato is placed in pure water (Ψ = 0 bars, Ψp = 0), calculate the pressure potential (Ψp) at equilibrium. Explain what this value represents in the context of plant cell turgor.

(c) Compare the response of a plant cell and an animal cell (e.g., a red blood cell) placed in each of the following solutions. Use appropriate terminology (plasmolysis, crenation, lysis, turgor, etc.):
    (i) A hypotonic solution
    (ii) A hypertonic solution

(d) Aquaporins are membrane protein channels that facilitate the movement of water across cell membranes. A researcher finds that certain plant cells in a drought-stressed leaf can reduce water loss by decreasing aquaporin expression.
    (i) Explain the mechanism by which aquaporins facilitate water movement without violating the passive nature of osmosis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Efficiency, phytoplankton→zooplankton: 42/500 = 8.4%. Efficiency, zooplankton→small fish: 4.2/42 = 10.0%. (ii) Three ways energy is lost: (1) Cellular respiration — a large fraction of ingested energy is used for metabolic processes (maintenance, thermoregulation in endotherms, movement) and released as heat → not available to next trophic level; (2) Excretion/urine/feces — some ingested organic matter passes through digestive tract unabsorbed and is lost in feces (egestion); urea and other nitrogenous waste products contain energy not passed up; (3) Not all organisms are consumed — some organisms die without being eaten → energy enters the decomposer food chain rather than the grazing food chain; (4) Reproduction and growth allocation — some energy is stored in tissues not consumed by the next trophic level (bones, shells, woody tissue). (iii) Three trophic levels above phytoplankton to reach tuna (tertiary consumer): phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. Mass of phytoplankton needed: 50 kg ÷ (0.1)³ = 50 ÷ 0.001 = 50,000 kg. 1 pt for correct efficiency calculations; 1 pt for tuna calculation with at least one energy loss explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate ecological efficiency between trophic levels; explain why < 10%; calculate phytoplankton needed for 50 kg tuna.
rubric.minimum_fix: Phytoplankton→zooplankton: 42/500 = 8.4%. Zooplankton→small fish: 4.2/42 = 10%. Energy lost as heat (respiration), feces (not absorbed), organisms not consumed. 50 kg tuna requires 50,000 kg phytoplankton (50 ÷ 0.1³).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete pathway: (1) N₂ (atmosphere) → NH₃/NH₄⁺: Nitrogen fixation. Organisms: free-living bacteria (Azotobacter) or symbiotic bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules). Enzyme: nitrogenase. N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ → NH₄⁺ in soil. (2) NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻: Nitrification. Organisms: Nitrosomonas (NH₄⁺→NO₂⁻) and Nitrobacter (NO₂⁻→NO₃⁻). (3) NO₃⁻ or NH₄⁺ absorbed by plant roots (active transport, via nitrate transporters). (4) NO₃⁻ → NH₄⁺: Nitrate reduction in plant (by nitrate reductase, using NADH/NADPH). (5) NH₄⁺ incorporated into amino acids: NH₄⁺ + α-ketoglutarate → glutamate (GS-GOGAT pathway in chloroplast); glutamate → other amino acids via transamination. (6) Amino acids assembled into proteins by ribosomes in leaf cells. Award 1 pt for correctly naming nitrogen fixation and nitrification with organisms; 1 pt for plant uptake, nitrate reduction, and amino acid synthesis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Trace a nitrogen atom from atmospheric N₂ to protein in a plant leaf cell, naming steps, organisms, and chemical forms.
rubric.minimum_fix: You have traced the overall pathway. To secure the second point, add the nitrate-reduction step: NO3- taken up by the roots is reduced back to NH4+ inside the plant before it is built into amino acids. Strengthen the answer further by naming the organisms - Rhizobium (fixation) and Nitrosomonas / Nitrobacter (nitrification).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) NPP = GPP − R. Tropical rainforest: 3300 − 2200 = 1100 g C/m²/yr. Temperate deciduous: 1200 − 800 = 400. Boreal forest: 700 − 500 = 200. Arctic tundra: 140 − 100 = 40. (ii) Tropical rainforest highest GPP despite smaller area than boreal because all four limiting factors are optimal: Light — year-round intense sunlight at low latitudes (near equator), no seasonal low-light winter; Temperature — warm year-round (25–30°C), optimal for enzyme function (photosynthesis enzymes); Water — high annual rainfall (2000+ mm), no water deficit limiting stomatal opening; Nutrient cycling — rapid decomposition in warm wet conditions means nutrients released quickly from dead organic matter and recycled rapidly into plant uptake. Boreal forests have seasonal darkness, cold temperatures (inhibit photosynthesis for months), frozen soil limiting nutrient access. 1 pt for all four NPP calculations correct; 1 pt for at least three of four explanatory factors for tropical GPP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate NPP for each biome; explain why tropical rainforest has highest GPP.
rubric.minimum_fix: NPP: Tropical=1100, Temperate=400, Boreal=200, Tundra=40 (g C/m²/yr). Tropical highest GPP: year-round intense sunlight (equatorial latitude), warm temperatures (optimal enzyme activity), high rainfall (no water deficit), rapid nutrient cycling (fast decomposition in warm-wet conditions).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete study design: Hypothesis: Removing the top predator (shark) from a coral reef reduces species diversity over 5 years. Measurements: (1) Species richness (number of species) and/or Shannon diversity index at the reef — baseline before shark removal and annually for 5 years. (2) Abundance of prey species (mesopredators like grouper, herbivores like parrotfish, urchins). (3) Coral cover percentage (as proxy for reef health). Method: Establish treatment reefs (sharks removed by fishing exclusion zones lifted or by simulated natural removal) and control reefs (sharks protected, same region). Survey via transect line/point counts at multiple sites annually. Statistical analysis: compare diversity metrics between treatment and control reefs over time, controlling for natural temporal variation. Determine result: if species richness/diversity index is significantly lower in shark-removed reefs than control reefs by year 5, prediction is supported. Limitation: any one of — (1) confounding variables (other human impacts, bleaching events) that could independently reduce diversity; (2) ethical/logistical challenges of actually removing sharks; (3) natural variation between reefs means differences may not be attributable to shark removal; (4) 5 years may be insufficient for cascade effects to be detectable. 1 pt for hypothesis + complete measurements + control/treatment structure; 1 pt for result determination criteria + specific limitation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Design a monitoring study to test the shark-removal prediction on coral reef species diversity.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypothesis: shark removal reduces coral reef species diversity. Measurements: annual species richness/diversity index surveys (transect counts) on shark-removed vs. control reefs. Results: compare diversity between reefs over 5 years; support if treatment reefs significantly less diverse. Limitation: confounding variables (bleaching, human fishing) may independently affect diversity and cannot be controlled.
