rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Bottleneck vs. selection: Bottleneck = random sampling event; when a population is dramatically reduced, only a small random sample of the original gene pool survives. Rare alleles are lost by chance regardless of their fitness value — loss is not based on phenotypic benefit/cost. Natural selection, by contrast, changes allele frequencies in a direction determined by fitness — it increases frequency of beneficial alleles and decreases frequency of harmful alleles. Bottleneck reduces diversity non-directionally (random alleles fixed or lost); selection changes diversity directionally (adaptive alleles favored). Result: a post-bottleneck population has low diversity across the genome, including at immune loci; post-selection population has adaptive alleles at high frequency but may retain diversity at neutral loci. (ii) Cheetah skin grafts: MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) genes determine self/non-self recognition in the immune system. Normally, unrelated individuals of the same species differ at MHC loci → immune cells detect MHC mismatch → reject transplanted tissue. Cheetahs can accept grafts from any other cheetah because the bottleneck reduced MHC diversity to near-zero — all cheetahs carry essentially the same MHC alleles → no immune mismatch → graft accepted. This reveals extreme genetic homogeneity; cheetahs are nearly as similar to each other as identical twins. This makes them vulnerable to epidemics. (iii) Elephant seal Ne paradox: Census size N = 170,000, but effective population size Ne was ~20 during the bottleneck. Ne is based on the breeding individuals and variance in reproductive success; the genetic diversity in the current population reflects the diversity that existed when Ne was at its minimum (~20 breeders). A population recovered from a recent bottleneck retains the low diversity of its bottleneck founders regardless of census size — recovery of numbers does not restore genetic variation lost during the bottleneck; only mutation over generations and gene flow can restore it. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly explained.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain bottleneck vs. selection; interpret cheetah skin grafts; explain elephant seal paradox with Ne.
rubric.minimum_fix: Bottleneck = random loss of alleles regardless of fitness (not directional). Selection = directional loss/gain based on fitness. Cheetah skin grafts: MHC diversity near zero → all cheetahs same MHC → no immune rejection. Elephant seal Ne paradox: current Ne still reflects the ~20 bottleneck founders; census size recovery does not restore genetic diversity lost during bottleneck.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Inbreeding depression mechanism: inbreeding (mating between relatives) increases the probability that an individual inherits the same allele from both parents (identity by descent) → increased homozygosity genome-wide. Most deleterious alleles are recessive and rare in outbred populations — they are mostly present in heterozygous individuals where the dominant allele masks the effect. In inbred individuals, probability of homozygosity for recessive deleterious alleles increases dramatically → deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (growth, fertility, survival, immunity). Purging hypothesis: in populations with prolonged inbreeding, the most severely deleterious recessive alleles may be "purged" — exposed in homozygotes and eliminated by natural selection. Mildly deleterious alleles are less efficiently purged because they have small fitness effects. (ii) Data interpretation for Population B: Population B has lower heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04), fewer alleles/locus (1.8 vs. 3.2), only 1 MHC allele (vs. 2), and higher frequency of morphological defects (kinked tail 85% vs. 50%; cryptic testes 90% vs. 55%). This indicates severe inbreeding. Predicted fitness consequences: high frequency of cryptic (undescended) testes → reduced male fertility → lower reproductive success; kinked tails (morphological defect, possibly spinal) → possible locomotion impairment in a predatory species; only 1 MHC allele → cannot recognize a diverse pathogen array → high susceptibility to infectious disease; low MHC diversity → poor immune response → epidemic vulnerability. Overall: inbreeding depression → low cub survival, poor reproductive performance, disease susceptibility.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain inbreeding depression mechanism; interpret panther data; predict fitness consequences.
rubric.minimum_fix: Inbreeding depression: increased homozygosity exposes recessive deleterious alleles → reduced fitness. Purging removes most severe alleles. Population B: lower heterozygosity, fewer alleles, 1 MHC allele, 85-90% morphological defects → predicted reduced fertility (cryptic testes), possible locomotion issues, severe disease susceptibility from single MHC allele.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Genetic rescue mechanism: introducing individuals from an outbred population provides new alleles not present in the inbred population. Crosses between inbred resident and outbred immigrant → offspring are heterozygous at many loci where residents are homozygous → dominant alleles mask previously exposed recessive deleterious alleles → fitness increases (heterosis/hybrid vigor). Also restores functional diversity at immune loci (MHC) → improved pathogen resistance. Effectively reverses inbreeding depression without changing the genome. (ii) Two risks: (1) Outbreeding depression: the introduced subspecies may carry alleles adapted to different Texas environments (different climate, prey, pathogens) that are maladaptive in Florida conditions; co-adapted gene complexes may be disrupted by hybridization → offspring less adapted to local environment than pure residents. (2) Genetic swamping: if Texas pumas are introduced in large numbers and have higher fitness (due to heterosis), their alleles could eventually replace the Florida panther genome entirely → the unique local adaptations and genetic identity of the Florida subspecies could be lost → "genetic extinction" even if population persists. (iii) Hybrid vs. pure offspring prediction: Hybrid offspring (puma × panther) will have higher heterozygosity than pure panther offspring → expect higher cub survival, fewer morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes), better immune function. This is heterosis (hybrid vigor) — the mechanism is complementation: the Texas puma alleles complement the Florida panther's recessive deleterious alleles, so the harmful homozygous recessive phenotypes are not expressed. Data from the 1995 introduction confirms: cub survival increased from 20% to 50%; defects declined dramatically. 1 pt for rescue mechanism; 1 pt for two risks OR hybrid prediction.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain genetic rescue mechanism; predict two risks; predict outcome of hybrid vs. pure offspring.
rubric.minimum_fix: Rescue mechanism: outbred immigrants → heterozygosity → recessive alleles masked → heterosis/hybrid vigor; new MHC alleles → better immunity. Risks: (1) outbreeding depression (maladapted Texas alleles in Florida); (2) genetic swamping (Florida genome replaced). Hybrid offspring: higher heterozygosity → heterosis → better survival, fewer defects; complementation masks deleterious recessive alleles.

accepted_variants: Ne ideal population genetic drift rate
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Effective population size (Ne): the size of an ideal panmictic population (random mating, equal sex ratio, equal reproductive success, no migration) that would experience the same rate of genetic drift (allele frequency change) as the actual population. Ne is almost always much smaller than census size N because: unequal sex ratio (e.g., 1 breeding male + 99 females → Ne ≈ 4, not 100); variance in reproductive success (dominant individuals breed much more than others → many individuals contribute no offspring → only a fraction effectively breed); fluctuating population sizes (Ne is dominated by the lowest N across generations — harmonic mean of past Ns); overlapping generations and age structure; geographic subdivision reducing effective breeding population. Typical Ne/N ratio in wildlife: 0.10–0.11. (ii) Two genetic risks below MVP: (1) Inbreeding depression: small populations have high relatedness → mating between relatives → homozygosity → recessive deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (fertility, immunity, survival). (2) Loss of adaptive potential (genetic erosion): genetic drift is strongest in small populations → neutral and mildly beneficial alleles lost by chance → allelic diversity decreases → population has fewer alleles available to respond to new selection pressures (disease outbreaks, climate change, new predators) → extinction risk increases. (iii) Genetic diversity for future change: a population with high genetic diversity has more heritable variation → when the environment changes (new pathogen, climate shift, habitat alteration), some individuals may already carry pre-existing alleles that confer survival advantage → natural selection can rapidly increase frequency of those alleles → population adapts and survives. A genetically uniform population (after bottleneck) has no variation for selection to act on → cannot adapt → high extinction risk. Genetic diversity = evolutionary raw material for adaptation. 1 pt per two of the four sub-parts correctly explained.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Define Ne; explain why Ne < N; describe two genetic risks below MVP; explain diversity for future change.
rubric.minimum_fix: Ne = effective population size (ideal population with same genetic drift rate). Ne < N due to: unequal sex ratio, variance in reproductive success, past bottlenecks (harmonic mean). Two genetic risks: inbreeding depression + genetic erosion (drift removes adaptive variation). Diversity for future: provides variation for selection to act on new challenges (disease, climate) → adaptation and survival.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies due to chance events.
    (i) Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs mechanistically from natural selection as a cause of reduced genetic diversity.
    (ii) A cheetah population experienced a severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago. Today, all cheetahs are nearly genetically identical and can accept skin grafts from any other cheetah without rejection. Explain why this is remarkable and what it reveals about the level of genetic diversity in the cheetah population.
    (iii) The northern elephant seal population dropped to ~20 individuals in the 1890s due to hunting and has since recovered to ~170,000 individuals. Despite this large census size, genetic diversity remains very low. Explain this paradox using the concept of effective population size (Ne).

(b) Inbreeding is common in small populations and can lead to inbreeding depression.
    (i) Explain the molecular mechanism of inbreeding depression. Include the roles of heterozygosity, recessive deleterious alleles, and the purging hypothesis.
    (ii) Table 1 shows genetic data for two Florida panther populations. Explain what the data indicate about genetic diversity and predict the fitness consequences for Population B.

(c) A conservation manager introduces 8 Texas pumas (a different subspecies) into the Florida panther population as a genetic rescue strategy.
    (i) Explain the mechanism by which genetic rescue increases fitness in an inbred population.
    (ii) Predict TWO risks of this genetic rescue strategy and explain why each is a concern.
    (iii) Five years after the introduction, the manager measures the heterozygosity and cub survival rate of offspring of puma-panther crosses versus pure panther offspring. Predict the outcome and the mechanism.

(d) Conservation biologists use the concept of minimum viable population (MVP) to determine the minimum population size needed to maintain a population long-term.
    (i) Define the effective population size (Ne) and explain why Ne is almost always much smaller than census size (N).
    (ii) Describe TWO genetic risks that threaten populations below the MVP threshold.
    (iii) Explain why maintaining genetic diversity is important for a species' long-term survival in a changing environment.

Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) alleles | 2 | 1

rubric.evidence_requirements: Pathway trace (multiple acceptable routes): (1) Atmosphere → Plants: CO₂ in atmosphere fixed by photosynthesis in autotrophs (plants, algae, cyanobacteria); CO₂ incorporated into organic molecules (glucose → starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids) in chloroplasts using light energy. Process: photosynthesis (Calvin cycle). (2) Plants → Consumers: plant tissue eaten by primary consumers (herbivores) → carbon in organic molecules transferred through food chain → passes to secondary consumers, etc. Process: consumption / ecological transfer. (3) Consumers/Plants → Atmosphere: cellular respiration in plants, animals, fungi, bacteria releases CO₂ back to atmosphere as organisms oxidize organic molecules for energy. Process: aerobic respiration, CO₂ released in Krebs cycle. (4) Dead organisms → Soil: dead organisms and waste decomposed by decomposers (bacteria, fungi) → CO₂ released to atmosphere (decomposition/mineralization); some carbon stored in soil organic matter (SOM) / humus. (5) Slow geological component: carbon buried in sediments → compressed over millions of years → fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas); or marine organisms with calcium carbonate shells die → shells accumulate → limestone (CaCO₃) rock. This takes millions of years and represents the slow geological carbon cycle. (6) Geological → Atmosphere: volcanic outgassing releases CO₂ from carbonate rock metamorphism; weathering of silicate rocks consumes CO₂. Human burning of fossil fuels short-circuits the slow geological cycle. 1 pt for at least 4 steps with organisms and processes named; 1 pt for including both fast biological and slow geological components.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Trace carbon atom through at least four cycle steps including both fast and slow components.
rubric.minimum_fix: At least 4 steps: CO₂ → photosynthesis (plants) → carbon in organic molecules → consumed by animals → respiration releases CO₂; or death → decomposers → CO₂. Slow component: burial → fossil fuels → millions of years; or limestone formation. Both fast (biological) and slow (geological) named.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) CO₂-temperature relationship: strong positive correlation — as CO₂ increased from 280 to 421 ppm (+50%), global temperature increased ~1.4°C. Greenhouse mechanism at molecular level: solar radiation (short wavelength visible light) passes through atmosphere → absorbed by Earth's surface → Earth re-emits longer wavelength infrared radiation (heat). CO₂ molecules (and CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) have molecular vibration modes (bending and stretching of C=O bonds) that absorb specific infrared wavelengths (CO₂ absorbs IR at ~15 μm) → CO₂ molecules re-emit IR in all directions, including back toward Earth → reduces energy escaping to space → atmospheric temperature increases (blanket effect). (ii) Fossil fuel disruption: Short-term (decades): burning releases CO₂ sequestered over millions of years → rapid spike in atmospheric CO₂ on timescale shorter than natural removal processes (ocean absorption, silicate weathering) → CO₂ builds up faster than it is removed. Geological timescale: fossil fuels represent carbon removed from the atmosphere during the Carboniferous Period (~360-300 Mya) by photosynthesis → reducing atmospheric CO₂ from >1000 ppm to present-day levels over millions of years. Burning reverses this in centuries. (iii) Positive feedback example: Permafrost thaw — Arctic permafrost contains ~1,500-1,600 Pg C (frozen organic matter from thousands of years). As global temperature rises: permafrost thaws → previously frozen organic matter exposed to microbial decomposition → decomposers release CO₂ and CH₄ (methane, 25× more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ over 100 years) → atmospheric greenhouse gases increase → more warming → more permafrost thaws → more CH₄/CO₂ released. This is self-reinforcing (positive feedback) because the output (warming) amplifies the input (warming). Positive feedback: initial warming → more permafrost thaw → more CH₄/CO₂ → more warming. 1 pt for greenhouse mechanism; 1 pt for positive feedback with mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe CO₂-temperature relationship and greenhouse mechanism; explain fossil fuel disruption; describe positive feedback.
rubric.minimum_fix: CO₂-temperature strong positive correlation. Greenhouse: CO₂ absorbs infrared (IR) re-emitted by Earth → re-emits back → traps heat. Fossil fuels: release millions of years of sequestered carbon in centuries → faster than removal; reverses Carboniferous carbon burial. Positive feedback: warming → permafrost thaws → CO₂/CH₄ released → more warming (self-reinforcing).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Chemistry sequence: CO₂(aq) + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid); H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate); HCO₃⁻ → H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ (carbonate). Net result: dissolving CO₂ releases H⁺ ions → ocean pH decreases. The pH has dropped from 8.25 to 8.10 (40% increase in H⁺, since pH is logarithmic). Acidification also drives the equilibrium: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻ → carbonate ions consumed → less carbonate available. (ii) Two consequences: (A) Calcification impairment: corals, mollusks, sea urchins, pteropods, and calcareous plankton (coccolithophores, foraminifera) build shells/skeletons from calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Lower pH = lower CO₃²⁻ concentration (consumed by H⁺) → aragonite and calcite saturation state decreases → organisms cannot precipitate CaCO₃ fast enough → thinner shells, dissolution of existing shells → impaired structural integrity, growth, and survival. Coral bleaching is exacerbated by acidification. (B) CO₂ narcosis / physiological acid-base disruption: marine fish and invertebrates regulate blood pH for enzyme function; excess CO₂ dissolving in body fluids = respiratory acidosis → disrupts acid-base balance → neurological effects (altered behavior, impaired predator avoidance) → reduced survival; disrupted fertilization and larval development. (iii) Feedback on CO₂ absorption: as ocean acidifies: CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻ shift reduces the ocean's buffering capacity; also, if calcifying organisms decline or die → less biogenic CaCO₃ sedimentation → less carbon buried in sediments (biological pump weakened) → less carbon removed from upper ocean → reduced capacity to absorb atmospheric CO₂. Positive feedback: more CO₂ → acidification → impaired biological pump → less CO₂ absorbed → more CO₂ in atmosphere → more warming. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly addressed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Write ocean acidification chemistry; describe two organism consequences; predict CO₂ absorption feedback.
rubric.minimum_fix: Chemistry: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H⁺ + CO₃²⁻; H⁺ increases → pH drops. Consequences: (1) calcification impaired (less CO₃²⁻ → thinner shells in corals, mollusks); (2) respiratory acidosis in fish (CO₂ in body fluids, altered behavior). Feedback: acidification weakens biological pump → less CO₂ absorbed → positive feedback.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Evaluation of strategies: Strategy 1 (Clear-cut + monoculture): Clear-cutting releases stored carbon immediately as debris decomposes and soil carbon is lost → large pulse of CO₂ emissions. Monocultures have low structural diversity → low carbon density in understory, soil, and woody debris; fast-growing trees fix carbon quickly but store less total carbon (smaller trees, less belowground carbon); monocultures are vulnerable to disease and pests → risk of catastrophic carbon release. NOT recommended for maximum long-term carbon storage. Strategy 2 (Selective harvest + diverse natural forest): maintains forest structure and continuous canopy cover → minimizes soil disturbance and carbon loss; selective harvest creates gaps that stimulate new growth → continuous carbon uptake; diverse structure supports high soil carbon (diverse root systems and litter inputs); more resilient to disturbance. Moderate carbon storage per hectare, but sustainable long-term. Strategy 3 (Protect old-growth as carbon reserve): old-growth forests have the highest carbon stocks per hectare — large-diameter trees have enormous woody biomass; dead wood (snags, fallen logs) stores carbon for decades; deep organic soils with high carbon content; carbon continues to accrue slowly even in old-growth (contrary to the misconception that mature forests are carbon neutral). Old-growth also has co-benefits (biodiversity, water regulation, climate buffering). Recommendation: Strategy 3 (old-growth protection) maximizes long-term carbon storage because: old-growth forests store more carbon per hectare than younger forests; protecting them avoids catastrophic emissions from disturbance; regeneration after clear-cutting takes decades to centuries to restore equivalent carbon stocks. Strategy 2 is a reasonable alternative if sustainable yield is required. 1 pt for evaluation of all three; 1 pt for recommendation with biological justification.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Evaluate three forest carbon strategies and recommend one with biological justification.
rubric.minimum_fix: Strategy 1: clear-cut releases stored carbon, monocultures low diversity/resilience — NOT recommended. Strategy 2: selective harvest maintains structure, soil carbon, continuous uptake — moderate. Strategy 3: old-growth has highest carbon stocks (large trees, deep soils, dead wood), continues to sequester, no emissions — BEST for long-term storage. Recommendation: protect old-growth; alternatives take centuries to match old-growth carbon density.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Trace the pathway of a single carbon atom as it cycles through the major components of the carbon cycle. Begin with CO₂ in the atmosphere and describe at least FOUR steps in the cycle, identifying the biological processes and organisms involved at each step. Include both the fast (biological) and slow (geological) components of the carbon cycle.

(b) Atmospheric CO₂ concentration has increased from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm today, largely due to burning fossil fuels.
    (i) Using Figure 1 data (atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature, 1850–2024), describe the relationship between CO₂ and global temperature. Explain the greenhouse effect mechanism at the molecular level.
    (ii) Explain why burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle at both short-term (decades) and geological-time (millions of years) timescales.

(c) When CO₂ dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid.
    (i) Write the complete chemical reaction sequence from CO₂ dissolution to hydrogen ion release. Explain how this leads to ocean acidification.

(d) A land manager must choose between three strategies to maximize long-term carbon storage in a 1000-hectare forest. Evaluate each strategy using your knowledge of carbon cycling:

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Primary succession. Justification: the eruption created entirely new substrate (volcanic rock, ash) devoid of any organisms or soil — there is no pre-existing biological legacy (no seedbank, no soil organic matter, no residual plant roots). Primary succession begins on bare, lifeless substrate; secondary succession begins where an existing community was disturbed but biological remnants remain (soil, seeds, roots). (ii) Facilitation model: early colonist species (pioneer species) arrive first, establish, modify the abiotic environment in ways that make it more hospitable for other species, and are eventually replaced by later-successional species they facilitated. At Mt. St. Helens: pioneer species include cyanobacteria and lichens (which fix atmospheric nitrogen → add N to bare substrate) and lupines (Lupinus lepidus — a nitrogen-fixing legume that colonized the pumice plain). Lupines: fix N₂ via Rhizobium symbiosis → add organic matter to barren substrate → create pockets of nutrient-rich soil → enable grasses and later shrubs to establish. Over time: accumulated organic matter → soil formation → more species can establish. Each wave of species facilitates the next. (iii) Diversity change: Years 0-5: very low species richness (only pioneer species tolerate bare substrate — cyanobacteria, lichens, specialized plants). Years 5-20: rising diversity as pioneer species modify substrate; mid-successional species colonize (grasses, forbs, early shrubs); overall diversity increases. Years 20-50: continued increase in diversity as forest species establish; eventually slowing as competitive exclusion and dominance by late-successional species begins to reduce diversity. IDH prediction: diversity may peak at intermediate stages before late-successional dominance reduces it. 1 pt for primary succession with correct justification; 1 pt for facilitation with pioneer species example.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify Mt. St. Helens succession; describe facilitation model; explain diversity change over time.
rubric.minimum_fix: Primary succession: bare substrate, no soil, no biological legacy. Facilitation: pioneer species (cyanobacteria/lichens or lupines) → fix N, add organic matter → enable later species. Diversity: low at first, increases as facilitation builds soil, then may slow as late-successional dominants compete. Lupines or N-fixing pioneers named.

accepted_variants: intermediate wave energy highest coral diversity
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Low diversity in undisturbed communities: without disturbance, competitive dominants monopolize resources over time → competitive exclusion drives inferior competitors to local extinction → the community becomes dominated by one or a few superior competitors → diversity declines. This is the expected endpoint of community succession toward climax (competitive equilibrium). Competitive exclusion: one species can drive another extinct if they compete for the same limited resource. (ii) Low diversity in highly disturbed communities: frequent or intense disturbance eliminates most species that cannot tolerate or recover from disturbance → only stress-tolerators or r-selected species (high dispersal, fast reproduction) can persist → few species → low diversity. Many species cannot complete life cycles before the next disturbance kills them. (iii) Intermediate disturbance maximizes diversity: intermediate disturbance creates patches where competitive dominants are eliminated → freed habitat colonized by new colonists including poor competitors → diversity high. Two processes coexist: competitive exclusion (favors late-successional specialists) and disturbance-mediated patch renewal (maintains space for early colonists and intermediate species). Disturbance prevents any single dominant from monopolizing → diverse "fugitive species" coexist with competitive dominants. Diversity is maximized because no single competitive dominant has time to exclude all others, but disturbance is not so frequent that only stress-tolerators persist. (iv) Coral reefs: intermediate wave disturbance (storms, wave action) creates open patches on the reef → pioneer coral species colonize → before competitive dominant corals (massive corals) can overgrow, another disturbance opens new patches → diverse coral species coexist at different patch ages. Reefs with intermediate wave energy → highest coral diversity. 1 pt for undisturbed + highly disturbed explanation; 1 pt for intermediate mechanism + reef application.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain IDH: why undisturbed is low diversity, disturbed is low, and intermediate is high; apply to coral reefs.
rubric.minimum_fix: Undisturbed: competitive exclusion → dominants reduce diversity. Highly disturbed: only stress-tolerators/r-selected persist → low diversity. Intermediate: competitive dominants eliminated periodically → patch renewal → fugitive species coexist → highest diversity. Coral reefs: intermediate wave disturbance creates diverse patch mosaic; prevents coral competitive exclusion.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Paine's Pisaster removal: when Paine removed all sea stars (Pisaster) from the experimental plot, mussels (Mytilus) — the primary prey of Pisaster and the competitive dominant — rapidly spread and covered all available rock surface → mussels competitively excluded barnacles, limpets, chitons, whelks, and other intertidal species → species richness declined dramatically from ~15 to ~1 species (mussel monoculture). Control plots (with Pisaster) maintained ~15 species. (ii) Keystone species definition: a species that has a disproportionately large effect on its community relative to its abundance — removing it causes dramatic changes in community structure (diversity, composition). Pisaster represented only a small fraction of intertidal biomass but controlled the dominant competitor. Trophic cascade mechanism: keystone predator (Pisaster) preys on dominant competitor (mussels) → keeps mussel population in check → prevents competitive exclusion of inferior species → multiple inferior competitors coexist. Remove predator → dominant competitor released from top-down control → exponential growth of dominant → competitive exclusion of all other species → diversity collapses. The cascade flows down from the top predator through the food web. (iii) Terrestrial example: wolves in Yellowstone National Park are keystone species. Wolves prey on elk → regulate elk numbers and behavior (elk avoid certain habitats when wolves present) → reduced elk browsing → recovery of willows, aspens, cottonwoods in riparian areas → beavers return → beaver dams create wetlands → increased bird species, fish, amphibians. This is a trophic cascade triggered by reintroduction of wolves in 1995. 1 pt for Pisaster experiment interpretation; 1 pt for keystone + trophic cascade + terrestrial example.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain Pisaster removal effect; define keystone and trophic cascade; give terrestrial example.
rubric.minimum_fix: Pisaster removal: mussels dominate → competitive exclusion of 15 species → diversity collapses to monoculture. Keystone species: disproportionate community effect relative to abundance; trophic cascade: predator controls dominant competitor → diversity maintained; remove predator → dominant explodes → exclusion. Terrestrial example: wolves in Yellowstone (control elk → allow riparian vegetation recovery).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Three ecological impacts of zebra mussels: (1) Filter feeding and phytoplankton depletion: zebra mussels are extremely efficient filter feeders (one mussel can filter up to 1 liter/day); dense populations (up to 700,000/m²) filter massive quantities of phytoplankton → water clarity increases dramatically but phytoplankton community collapses → zooplankton that depend on phytoplankton decline → food web base disrupted → native fish (whitefish, cisco) that eat zooplankton decline. (2) Competition with native bivalves: native unionid mussels (clams) cannot compete with zebra mussel density; zebra mussels attach to native clam shells, physically smothering and competing for food → native freshwater mussel species (many endangered) dramatically decline → 37+ species of unionid mussels in Great Lakes threatened. (3) Biofouling and infrastructure damage: zebra mussels attach to boat hulls, water intake pipes, underwater structures → clog municipal water intakes → cost billions of dollars; alter substrate availability for other benthic organisms. (ii) Invasive success reasons: released from natural enemies (predators, pathogens, parasites that controlled population in native range); novel ecosystem lacks co-evolved competitors → reduced interspecific competition; high reproductive rate (r-selected); high phenotypic plasticity → adapt to wide range of conditions; accidental or intentional introduction provides propagule pressure. (iii) Ecologically sound management: biological control — identify and introduce a specialist predator or parasite from the native Eurasian range that targets zebra mussels without harming native species. Example: the diving duck Aythya ferina (common pochard) preferentially eats Dreissena in Europe; or research into native crayfish that may prey on juveniles. Mechanism: natural enemy → top-down population control → long-term suppression without chemicals. Chemical control (e.g., chlorine, potassium chloride) is ecologically harmful to non-target species. Accept any biologically sound strategy with mechanism. 1 pt for three impacts; 1 pt for invasive success + management strategy.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe three zebra mussel impacts; explain invasive success; propose management strategy.
rubric.minimum_fix: Three impacts: (1) filter feeding depletes phytoplankton → food web disruption; (2) native unionid mussel competition/smothering; (3) biofouling infrastructure. Invasive success: no natural enemies, reduced competition, high reproduction. Management: biological control (native-range predator/parasite) for long-term suppression without chemical harm.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, destroying 600 km² of forest and depositing meters of volcanic ash and rock. Ecologists have monitored species recovery in this area since 1980.
    (i) Classify the ecological succession occurring at Mount St. Helens as primary or secondary, and justify your classification.
    (ii) Describe the facilitiation model of succession and apply it to the Mount St. Helens recovery. Name a specific type of early colonist (pioneer species) and explain how it modifies the environment to make it suitable for later species.
    (iii) Describe how species diversity (as measured by the Shannon diversity index or species richness) would change over succession time from year 0 to year 50 at Mount St. Helens. Explain the mechanism.
items.stimulus:
(b) The intermediate disturbance hypothesis (IDH) predicts that species diversity is highest at intermediate levels of disturbance frequency and intensity.
    (i) Explain why diversity is lower in undisturbed communities. What process dominates in the absence of disturbance?
    (ii) Explain why diversity is also lower in highly disturbed communities. What types of species persist?
    (iii) Explain why intermediate disturbance maximizes diversity. Use the concept of competitive exclusion in your answer.
    (iv) Predict how the IDH applies to coral reefs, where wave disturbance creates patches of open substrate.

(c) Keystone species have a disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to their abundance. Robert Paine's classic experiment with sea stars (Pisaster ochraceus) in Pacific tidepools demonstrated this.
    (i) Explain what happened to species diversity when Paine removed Pisaster from the tidal zone.
    (ii) Define keystone species and explain the trophic cascade mechanism by which losing a keystone predator causes loss of biodiversity.
    (iii) Give ONE example of a keystone species in a terrestrial ecosystem (not Pisaster) and explain its role.

(d) Invasive species are a leading cause of native species extinction. The invasive zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha) was introduced into the Great Lakes in 1988 via ballast water.
    (i) Describe THREE ecological impacts of zebra mussels on the Great Lakes ecosystem.
    (ii) Explain why invasive species often succeed so dramatically in their introduced environment.
    (iii) Propose ONE ecologically sound management strategy for zebra mussels and explain its mechanism.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Mutualism (+/+): both partners benefit. Example: mycorrhizal fungi + plant roots (fungus gets photosynthate/sugars; plant gets water/phosphorus via extended hyphal network). Or: nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium in legume root nodules; pollinator-flower (bee gets nectar/pollen; flower gets pollination). Obligate in many cases (neither partner survives or reproduces as well without the other); some are facultative. Evolutionary implication: reciprocal positive selection pressure → coevolution of mutual dependence; both species' fitness increases with the other's presence → selection favors stronger partnership → can lead to irreversible co-dependence. Commensalism (+/0): one benefits, the other is neither helped nor harmed. Example: barnacles on whale skin (barnacles get transport and access to food; whale unaffected). Or: cattle egrets following grazing cattle (egrets benefit from insects disturbed by cattle; cattle unaffected). Usually facultative. Evolutionary implication: commensal may evolve traits that better exploit the host; if the host eventually bears a cost, commensalism slides toward parasitism. Parasitism (+/−): parasite benefits, host harmed. Example: Plasmodium (malaria parasite) in human host; tapeworms in vertebrate gut; mistletoe on trees. Obligate for many. Evolutionary implication: coevolutionary arms race — host evolves defenses (immune recognition), parasite evolves countermeasures (immune evasion) → Red Queen dynamics. Award 1 pt for two symbiosis types with all four elements; 1 pt for the third.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism with effects, examples, obligate/facultative, and evolutionary implication.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mutualism (+/+): mycorrhizae or bee-flower; both benefit; can be obligate; coevolve mutual dependence. Commensalism (+/0): barnacles on whale; one benefits, other unaffected; usually facultative; commensal may drift to parasitism. Parasitism (+/−): Plasmodium in human; parasite benefits, host harmed; often obligate; Red Queen arms race.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Mycorrhizal mutualism mechanism: The plant contributes: photosynthetically produced carbohydrates (sugars, sucrose) transported to fungal partner via phloem to root, then across the symbiotic interface to the fungus. The fungus contributes: extensive hyphal network that extends far beyond the plant's root system → vastly increases the effective soil volume explored for water and mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N). Fungal hyphae are much thinner than roots → can penetrate soil pores inaccessible to roots → access P bound to soil particles; hyphae secrete phosphatases to mineralize organic P. The fungus delivers P and water to the plant via the symbiotic interface (periarbuscular membrane in arbuscular mycorrhizae) in exchange for sugars. (ii) Data analysis: Benefit is greatest at very low P (463% increase) and decreases as soil P increases until at high P only 2% benefit. Explanation: when soil P is scarce, the plant cannot absorb sufficient P through its own roots → severely P-limited → fungal hyphae provide essential P access → huge growth benefit. At high soil P: plant can absorb P directly through roots without fungal help → fungal phosphorus delivery is redundant → plant gains little from the relationship, but still pays cost in photosynthate → net benefit minimal. (iii) Mutualism-parasitism continuum / cheaters: under high nutrient conditions (high P, high N), the plant has little to gain from mycorrhizae but still pays carbon to the fungus → relationship shifts toward parasitism (fungus benefits more than plant, plant bears net cost). Cheating fungi: some fungal strains fail to deliver adequate P to the plant while still receiving carbon → "parasitic" cheater strategies; in lab, some Glomus strains become net negative in high P soils. The relationship is context-dependent; not a fixed mutualism. 1 pt for mechanism; 1 pt for data analysis and cheater explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain mycorrhizal mechanism; analyze phosphorus data; explain cheater conditions.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mechanism: plant gives sugars; fungus gives phosphorus and water via extensive hyphae inaccessible to roots. Data: greatest benefit at low P (fungus essential for P uptake); minimal benefit at high P (plant absorbs P directly). Cheating: at high P, fungus gains carbon but delivers little P → shifts toward parasitism; some fungal strains become net negative cheaters.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Red Queen hypothesis: parasites co-evolve with hosts in an ongoing arms race where neither side "wins" — both must constantly evolve just to maintain their relative fitness (like the Red Queen in Alice in Wonderland who runs constantly just to stay in place). Frequency-dependent selection: parasites evolve to infect the most COMMON host genotype (because infecting rare genotypes is not adaptively favored); when a common host genotype is heavily parasitized → fitness decreases → its frequency declines; a rare genotype that parasites cannot yet infect → escapes parasitism → increases in frequency → eventually becomes common → parasites evolve to infect it → cycle continues. Advantage of sexual reproduction: sexual reproduction continuously generates new genotype combinations (through recombination and independent assortment) → rare genotypes continuously produced → one step ahead of parasites. Asexual populations produce clonal offspring (identical genotype) → once parasite evolves to infect the common clone, all offspring are vulnerable → high susceptibility. This "tangled bank" hypothesis predicts sexual reproduction is adaptive in environments with abundant coevolving parasites. Empirical support: New Zealand snail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum) populations with heavy parasite loads have higher rates of sexual reproduction than populations in low-parasite environments. (ii) Newt-snake arms race: Newts produce TTX (tetrodotoxin) → blocks voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) → prevents action potential conduction → paralysis and death of most predators. Garter snakes that eat newts have evolved resistance alleles in the SCN4A gene (encodes Nav1.4 sodium channel subunit) → point mutations change the TTX-binding site on the channel → TTX cannot bind effectively → channels remain functional → snake survives eating newt. Arms race: populations with higher newt TTX → selection for snakes with higher Nav resistance → snakes develop resistance → newts face selection for higher TTX production → escalation cycle. Geographic variation: coastal Oregon populations co-occur with highly toxic newts → snakes have highest TTX resistance allele frequencies; inland populations rarely encounter toxic newts → low resistance allele frequency → "geographic mosaic of coevolution." 1 pt for Red Queen + frequency-dependent selection + sexual reproduction; 1 pt for newt-snake molecular mechanism + geographic variation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain Red Queen hypothesis with frequency-dependent selection and sexual reproduction; describe newt-snake arms race.
rubric.minimum_fix: Red Queen: ongoing arms race; parasites evolve to infect common host → common genotype declines → rare escapes → becomes common → cycle. Sexual reproduction advantage: produces new genotypes faster than asexual clones → harder for parasites to keep up. Newt-snake: newt TTX blocks sodium channels; snake SCN4A mutations reduce TTX binding → resistance; higher TTX newts → more resistance snakes → arms race; coastal Oregon highest co-evolution.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Example: Wolbachia bacteria → mitochondria (endosymbiosis evolution): Ancestral interaction: ancient alpha-proteobacterium was initially an intracellular parasite/pathogen of a proto-eukaryotic cell — extracting energy and nutrients from the host cell → parasitic antagonistic relationship (bacterium +, host −). Selective pressures on the host: selection favored host cells that could tolerate the intracellular bacterium without dying, or that extracted metabolic benefit from bacterial energy production (oxidative phosphorylation capacity). Selective pressures on the bacterium: selection favored less virulent strains that did not kill their host too quickly (enhanced transmission if host survives longer; vertical transmission through cell division). Genetic and phenotypic changes: (1) Bacterium → reduced genome (non-essential genes lost; genes transferred to host nucleus); (2) Host → evolved protein import machinery (TOM/TIM complexes) to import nuclear-encoded proteins into bacterium; (3) Both → evolved complementary metabolite exchange (bacterium exports ATP; host exports substrates). Evolutionary transition: as bacteria became increasingly dependent on host-imported proteins and less able to survive outside the cell, and as host became dependent on bacterial ATP, the relationship shifted from parasitism → commensalism (bacterium neutral effect) → mutualism (both benefit → mitochondria/chloroplasts). This is endosymbiotic theory. Other examples: cleaning stations (cleaner wrasse originally eat skin parasites off fish → possible mutualism from kleptoparasitism); fig-fig wasp mutualism (from parasite that laid eggs in flowers). Accept any well-reasoned pathway. 1 pt for ancestral antagonistic relationship + selective pressures; 1 pt for genetic changes + evolutionary transition with mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe evolutionary pathway from antagonism to mutualism with ancestral interaction, selection, genetic changes, and transition.
rubric.minimum_fix: Ancestral antagonism: intracellular parasite (α-proteobacterium) in proto-eukaryote. Selection: host tolerates bacterium if gains ATP; bacterium less virulent if host survives longer. Genetic changes: bacterial genome reduced, host import machinery (TOM/TIM) evolved, protein transfer to nucleus. Transition: parasite → commensal → mutualist (mitochondria) as mutual dependence increased. Endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Symbiosis describes close ecological relationships between two species. Compare mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism using the following framework for each: (i) effect on each partner (+ or −); (ii) specific biological example; (iii) whether the relationship is obligate or facultative; and (iv) one evolutionary implication of the relationship.

(b) Mycorrhizal fungi form mutualistic associations with the roots of over 90% of plant species.
    (i) Describe the mechanism of the mycorrhizal mutualism — explain specifically what each partner contributes to and receives from the relationship.
    (ii) The data in Table 1 show plant growth with and without mycorrhizal fungi at different phosphorus soil levels. Analyze these data and explain why the mutualistic benefit is greatest under low phosphorus conditions.
    (iii) Explain whether mycorrhizal associations are truly mutualistic or whether they lie on a mutualism-parasitism continuum. Describe the conditions under which mycorrhizal fungi might become "cheaters" (gaining resources without providing benefit).

(c) Coevolution occurs when two species exert reciprocal selective pressure on each other, each evolving in response to the other.
    (i) The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that parasites drive ongoing coevolution with their hosts. Explain this hypothesis, using the concept of frequency-dependent selection. Include why sexual reproduction may be advantageous in coevolving host-parasite systems.
    (ii) Describe the coevolutionary arms race between the rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) and its predator, the common garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis). Explain the molecular mechanism involved and the geographic variation observed.

(d) Describe a plausible evolutionary pathway by which a mutualistic symbiosis could have originated from a parasitic or antagonistic relationship. Your answer should include: the ancestral interaction, the selective pressures acting on both species, specific genetic/phenotypic changes, and the evolutionary transition from antagonism to mutualism. You may use any pair of organisms as your example.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: Plant growth (dry mass, grams) with and without mycorrhizal fungi (MF)
Soil phosphorus level | Without MF | With MF | Benefit (% increase)
    Very low           |    0.8 g   |  4.5 g  |       +463%
    Low                |    1.4 g   |  5.2 g  |       +271%
    Medium             |    3.0 g   |  4.8 g  |        +60%
    High               |    4.5 g   |  4.6 g  |         +2%

Rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) toxicity:
• Newts produce tetrodotoxin (TTX) — a potent sodium channel blocker
• TTX blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevents action potential propagation → paralysis, death
• Some garter snake populations have evolved Na⁺ channel mutations (in SCN4A gene) that reduce TTX binding
• Population variation: Oregon coastal garter snakes (high TTX resistance) vs. inland snakes (low resistance)

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Island size and extinction rate: larger islands support larger population sizes for each species → larger populations have lower extinction probability (lower demographic stochasticity, lower genetic drift, can absorb environmental fluctuation). Smaller islands → smaller populations → higher extinction rate per species → fewer species at equilibrium. Also, larger islands offer more habitat types/niches → support more species. Mechanism: extinction rate decreases with increasing island area; immigration rate is roughly independent of island size → larger island has lower extinction rate relative to immigration rate → higher equilibrium species richness. (ii) Island distance and immigration rate: more distant islands are reached by fewer colonists from mainland because dispersal probability decreases with distance (many organisms cannot travel far; propagule survival declines with distance). Lower immigration rate on distant islands → fewer new species arrive per year → fewer new arrivals to replace extinct species → lower equilibrium species richness. Near islands: higher immigration → more arrivals → more colonizations per year → higher equilibrium. Mechanism: immigration rate decreases with increasing distance; extinction rate is distance-independent → near islands achieve higher equilibrium than far islands. (iii) Species-area calculation: S = CA^z. If area is halved: S_new = C(A/2)^z = CA^z × (1/2)^z = S_original × (1/2)^0.25. (1/2)^0.25 = 2^(-0.25) = 1/2^0.25 ≈ 1/1.189 ≈ 0.841. New S ≈ 84.1% of original. Halving the area reduces species richness to ~84% (a ~16% reduction in species) — not 50%, because the species-area relationship is sublinear (z < 1). 1 pt per correct mechanism (size + distance); 1 pt for calculation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain island size → extinction rate; distance → immigration rate; calculate effect of halving area.
rubric.minimum_fix: Size → larger populations → lower extinction rate → more species. Distance → lower immigration rate → fewer colonists → fewer species. Calculation: S_new = S × (1/2)^0.25 = S × 0.841; species richness drops to ~84% (≈16% loss) when area is halved — NOT proportional because z < 1.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Three fragmentation effects beyond area: (1) Edge effects: fragmentation increases the ratio of edge habitat to interior habitat; edge habitat has altered abiotic conditions (higher light, temperature, wind, drying) and is invaded by edge-tolerant and invasive species → interior species cannot survive in edge zones → effective interior habitat much smaller than total patch area → loss of area-sensitive species (many forest birds nest only in deep interior). (2) Reduced connectivity and gene flow: isolated patches → no immigration between patches → populations cannot receive new alleles → inbreeding within isolated populations → inbreeding depression + loss of adaptive variation → higher local extinction risk. (3) Barrier to movement and dispersal: organisms cannot move between isolated patches → recolonization of a patch after local extinction is impossible (rescue effect eliminated) → once a species goes locally extinct in a patch, it is permanently lost from that patch. Also, migration for seasonal resources prevented. (ii) SLOSS debate: Arguments for Single Large (SL): large reserves contain more interior habitat → fewer edge effects; support larger populations per species → lower extinction rates; can accommodate species with large home ranges (large carnivores, wide-ranging birds); can harbor more total species due to species-area relationship; contain complete ecological communities including rare interior-specialist species. Arguments for Several Small (SS): multiple reserves hedge against catastrophic single events (disease, fire, pollution, invasive species) — if all individuals are in one reserve, a single event can cause total extinction; several reserves can protect species with different habitat requirements; can cover more geographic area and therefore more habitat types; provide redundancy. Empirical evidence: generally favors SL for maximizing species richness, especially for large, area-sensitive species; however, SS may be superior in practice for population viability (insurance against catastrophe). No universal winner — landscape context matters. (iii) Wildlife corridor mechanism: corridors allow individuals to move between otherwise isolated patches → restores gene flow between patches → prevents inbreeding depression; allows recolonization after local extinction (rescue effect) → population can recover from disease or stochastic events in one patch; allows seasonal migration; expands effective population size (Ne) by connecting subpopulations into a metapopulation → reduces individual patch extinction probability. Functionally, corridors convert an "island" landscape into a metapopulation network. 1 pt for three edge/connectivity/barrier effects; 1 pt for SLOSS arguments; 1 pt for corridor mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain three fragmentation effects beyond area loss; argue SLOSS; explain corridor mechanism.
rubric.minimum_fix: Three effects: (1) edge effects (interior habitat loss, edge-adapted invaders); (2) reduced gene flow and inbreeding in isolated patches; (3) no recolonization after local extinction (rescue effect lost). SLOSS: SL → more interior species, larger populations; SS → insurance against catastrophe, geographic spread. Empirical: usually SL wins for species richness. Corridors: restore gene flow, rescue effect (recolonization), expand effective metapopulation size.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Patch A + corridor: (1) Island biogeography rescue effect: corridor to Patch B allows immigration of new individuals → if ferret population in A declines, individuals from B can recolonize/supplement (rescue effect) → lower extinction probability; (2) Metapopulation dynamics: A and B are connected subpopulations within a metapopulation; recolonization maintains each patch population above minimum viable population threshold; (3) Gene flow: corridor allows exchange of individuals and alleles between A and B → prevents inbreeding; heterozygosity maintained → inbreeding depression avoided → cubs survive, reproduction high. Patch C isolated: (1) No rescue effect: if local extinction or severe decline occurs, no immigration possible → population cannot recover; stochastic events (disease outbreak: sylvatic plague from Yersinia could wipe out all prairie dogs → ferrets starve) → no recolonization; (2) Small isolated population → genetic drift + inbreeding → loss of MHC diversity → poor immune function → disease susceptibility → population crash; (3) Demographic stochasticity: with few founding individuals in isolated patch, sex ratio imbalance, loss of breeding individuals to accidents, etc., → population cannot sustain itself. The corridor provides the rescue effect, gene flow, and connectivity that Patch C lacks entirely → Patch C functions as a true ecological island with no immigration → expected outcome: eventual extinction following any perturbation. 1 pt for Patch A connectivity advantages (rescue effect + gene flow); 1 pt for Patch C isolation failure mechanisms.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why Patch A (connected) succeeded and Patch C (isolated) failed using island biogeography, metapopulation, and inbreeding.
rubric.minimum_fix: Patch A success: corridor provides rescue effect (recolonization from B if population declines), gene flow (prevents inbreeding, maintains fitness), metapopulation dynamics. Patch C failure: no immigration possible → no rescue effect; inbreeding → fitness decline; demographic stochasticity + sylvatic plague → extinction with no recovery.

accepted_variants: mountaintop island shrinks as temperature rises
no higher to go extinction risk
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Mountaintop species and island biogeography: as temperatures warm, suitable habitat shifts upslope → high-elevation species must track their thermal niche by moving upslope. Mountaintops are like true islands of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable warm lowland "sea." As the suitable thermal zone shifts up: the area of suitable habitat SHRINKS (mountain width decreases toward the summit → species-area relationship predicts fewer species can be supported → extinction risk increases). Eventually, the suitable zone disappears off the top of the mountain → complete habitat loss → extinction. Unlike lowland species, mountaintop species cannot move further north or to higher elevations without running out of mountain → climate-tracked range contraction leads to island shrinkage and eventual extinction. (ii) Demographic consequences for plant (800-1200 m → 1000-1400 m shift): Lower boundary shifts up to 1000 m → plants below 1000 m experience unsuitable thermal conditions → lower population declines as plants die or fail to reproduce at the trailing edge. Upper boundary shifts to 1400 m → plants above 1200 m (assuming they can disperse there) find new suitable habitat at leading edge. Net effect: if seeds can disperse upslope fast enough → population may shift range (but plants have limited dispersal). If dispersal insufficient → range shrinks as lower end contracts faster than upper end expands → population decline → extinction risk. Many plants cannot disperse 200 m in elevation fast enough to track a shifting thermal zone under rapid climate change. (iii) Two climate-aware conservation strategies: (1) Assisted migration (assisted colonization): deliberately translocate individuals to suitable habitats outside their current range that will be climatically suitable in the future. Moves species faster than they can disperse naturally; pre-emptively establishes populations in future range. Risk: potential invasive effects in recipient community. (2) Climate-adaptive reserve networks: identify and protect corridors along elevation gradients and latitudinal gradients → allow species to naturally migrate to track their climate niche; connect reserves from low to high elevation and south to north → functional corridors enable range shifts. Design reserves to include diverse elevation gradients within each reserve. 1 pt for mountaintop island biogeography explanation; 1 pt for demographic consequences OR two strategies.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain mountaintop extinction risk from climate; predict demographic consequences; describe two climate-aware conservation strategies.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mountaintops: suitable habitat shrinks as thermal zone shifts up → species-area → fewer species; no habitat beyond summit → extinction. Plant: lower range contracts (conditions unsuitable below 1000 m); upper range may expand if seeds can disperse to 1400 m; if dispersal too slow → range shrinks → decline. Strategies: (1) assisted migration; (2) elevation and latitudinal corridors for natural range tracking.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The MacArthur-Wilson theory of island biogeography predicts that species richness on an island represents a dynamic equilibrium between immigration and extinction rates.
    (i) Explain how island SIZE affects species richness. Describe the mechanism connecting island size to extinction rate.
    (ii) Explain how island DISTANCE from a mainland source pool affects species richness. Describe the mechanism connecting distance to immigration rate.
    (iii) Using the species-area relationship (S = CA^z, where S = number of species, A = area, C and z are constants), predict what happens to species richness if an island's effective area is halved. Use z = 0.25 in your calculation and express your answer as a percentage of the original species richness.

(b) Habitat fragmentation effectively converts contiguous habitat into island-like patches.
    (i) Explain THREE ways in which habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity beyond simply reducing total habitat area.
    (ii) The SLOSS debate asks whether conservation managers should prefer a Single Large (SL) or Several Small (SS) reserves of equivalent total area.
    Describe the ecological arguments for EACH side of the debate. Then state which side the empirical evidence most often supports and explain why.
    (iii) Explain the biological mechanism by which wildlife corridors connecting habitat patches maintain or increase biodiversity.

(c) A conservation biologist tracks the reintroduction of a locally extinct species (the black-footed ferret) into a fragmented prairie landscape. Three years after reintroduction into Patch A (large, connected to Patch B by a corridor), the ferret population is thriving. In Patch C (same size as A but isolated), the reintroduction failed. Explain the likely reasons for the difference in outcomes, using concepts from island biogeography, metapopulation theory, and inbreeding depression.

(d) Climate change is shifting species' geographic ranges poleward and to higher elevations.
    (i) Explain why mountaintop species face a greater extinction risk from climate change than lowland species, using island biogeography theory as a framework.
    (ii) A plant species currently has its range between 800–1200 m elevation. As temperatures warm, the suitable thermal range shifts to 1000–1400 m. Predict the demographic consequences for this population and explain whether the population can respond.
    (iii) Describe TWO conservation strategies that explicitly account for climate change in protecting biodiversity.

Island area (km²) | Number of bird species

  1,000            |          64
 10,000            |         112

From log-log plot: z ≈ 0.25, consistent with MacArthur-Wilson predictions
(z = 0.13-0.18 for mainland habitat patches; z = 0.25-0.35 for true oceanic islands)

SLOSS background:
• Species-area relationship: SL may contain more species (especially area-sensitive and interior species)
• Rescue effect: Several small patches may protect against catastrophic single-event extinction
• Edge effects: fragmented habitat has high perimeter-to-area ratio → more edge, less interior
• Minimum viable area: some species (large carnivores, area-sensitive forest birds) require a minimum patch size to persist

Black-footed ferret facts:

• Current population: ~300 individuals in the wild from reintroduction programs beginning 1991
• Highly sensitive to sylvatic plague (Yersinia pestis) — can kill entire ferret and prairie dog colonies

rubric.evidence_requirements: Vmax approximately 50 micromol/min (the plateau value approached at high substrate). Km is the substrate concentration at half-Vmax (approximately 25 micromol/min), which falls between 1.0 and 2.0 mM, roughly 1.5-2.0 mM. Accept reasonable estimates within range with correct method shown.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Estimate Vmax and Km from the data table.
rubric.minimum_fix: Vmax is about 50 micromol/min (the plateau); Km is the substrate concentration giving half that rate, roughly 1.5-2.0 mM.

rubric.evidence_requirements: At high substrate concentration, all (or nearly all) enzyme active sites are saturated/occupied at any given moment; the enzyme is working at its maximum turnover rate; adding more substrate cannot increase rate because no free active sites are available to bind it.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why reaction rate plateaus at high substrate concentration.
rubric.minimum_fix: At high substrate concentration the enzyme active sites are saturated, so the enzyme is working as fast as it can regardless of additional substrate.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Vmax stays the same (unchanged) because, given enough substrate, substrate will outcompete the inhibitor for the active site and full enzyme activity can still be achieved. Km increases (apparent Km is higher) because more substrate is needed to reach half-Vmax due to competition between substrate and inhibitor for the same active site.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how Vmax and Km change with a competitive inhibitor and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Vmax is unchanged because excess substrate can outcompete the inhibitor; Km increases because more substrate is needed to overcome competition for the active site.

accepted_variants: competitive inhibition is overcome at high [S]
rubric.evidence_requirements: At 50x Km, substrate concentration is high enough to outcompete the inhibitor for the active site; reaction rate approaches the same Vmax as the uninhibited reaction (approximately 50 micromol/min), because competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficiently high substrate concentration.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict reaction rate at very high substrate concentration with competitive inhibitor present.
rubric.minimum_fix: Reaction rate approaches the original Vmax (about 50 micromol/min) because the high substrate concentration outcompetes the inhibitor for active sites.

accepted_variants: noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere not active site
rubric.evidence_requirements: Repeat the substrate titration with the inhibitor present and compare to uninhibited curve: if Vmax is restored (unchanged) at high substrate but Km increases, inhibition is competitive. If Vmax is lower than uninhibited even at very high substrate concentration (Km roughly unchanged), inhibition is noncompetitive (inhibitor binds a site other than the active site and cannot be outcompeted by substrate).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Propose an experiment to distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition using reaction-rate data.
rubric.minimum_fix: Run the same substrate titration with the inhibitor present: if high substrate restores the original Vmax, the inhibition is competitive; if Vmax remains lowered even at high substrate, the inhibition is noncompetitive.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) (i) Using the data in the table, estimate the Vmax and Km of the uninhibited enzyme reaction.
    (ii) Explain why reaction rate plateaus at high substrate concentration even though substrate is not limiting.

(b) A competitive inhibitor is added at a fixed concentration and the experiment is repeated. Predict how Vmax and Km would change relative to the uninhibited reaction, and explain why, based on the mechanism of competitive inhibition.

(c) Researchers raise the substrate concentration to 50 times the original Km in the presence of the same competitive inhibitor. Predict what happens to reaction rate relative to the uninhibited Vmax and explain your reasoning.

(d) Propose a modification to the experiment that would distinguish a competitive inhibitor from a noncompetitive inhibitor using only reaction-rate data, and explain what result would confirm each mechanism.
