catabolite activator protein binds promoter region
rubric.evidence_requirements: When glucose is absent, adenylyl cyclase is active and cAMP levels rise; cAMP binds to CAP (catabolite activator protein); CAP-cAMP complex binds to the CAP site upstream of the lac promoter and stimulates RNA polymerase binding, increasing transcription of the structural genes — this is positive control on top of negative (repressor) control.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why glucose deprivation also increases lac operon expression (catabolite repression / positive control).
rubric.minimum_fix: Low glucose raises cAMP levels; cAMP-CAP complex binds upstream of the promoter and enhances RNA polymerase binding, increasing transcription of the lac structural genes.

items.stem: In E. coli, genes that encode lactose-metabolizing enzymes are controlled by the lac operon, a cluster of genes with shared regulatory sequences.
items.stimulus: A diagram shows the lac operon with the regulatory gene (lacI), promoter, operator, and structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA), plus the repressor protein and allolactose.

accepted_variants: independent evolution via mutation and selection
rubric.evidence_requirements: Geographic isolation (mountain range) prevents gene flow between populations; each population accumulates different mutations and evolves under different selection pressures; over time genetic differences accumulate to the point where the two groups can no longer interbreed successfully even if barriers were removed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how allopatric speciation could produce two distinct species from a single ancestral population.
rubric.minimum_fix: Physical separation prevented gene flow; each population independently accumulated genetic differences through mutation and natural selection; eventually reproductive isolation arose, producing two distinct species.

accepted_variants: prezygotic: behavioral, temporal, or mechanical isolation
rubric.evidence_requirements: Prezygotic: behavioral isolation (different mating displays or pheromones prevent courtship); or temporal isolation (different mating seasons); or mechanical isolation (incompatible genitalia). Postzygotic: hybrid inviability (hybrid offspring die before reproducing); or hybrid sterility (hybrids are sterile, as in the scenario).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe one prezygotic and one postzygotic reproductive isolating mechanism that could prevent interbreeding between the two lizard groups if they came back into contact.
rubric.minimum_fix: Prezygotic: behavioral isolation — the two groups do not recognize each other as potential mates, preventing mating attempts. Postzygotic: hybrid inviability — offspring from mixed-group matings have reduced survival or fertility.

items.stem: A mountain range formed 2 million years ago divided a formerly continuous lizard population into two geographically isolated groups.
items.stimulus: Present-day descendants of the two groups have morphological and behavioral differences. When brought into contact in the lab, they rarely interbreed and hybrids have reduced survival.

accepted_variants: energy not stored is lost as heat
rubric.evidence_requirements: Most energy consumed at each trophic level is lost as heat during cellular respiration; some is used for metabolism, growth, and reproduction; some is excreted as waste; only the energy stored in new biomass (approximately 10%) is available to the next trophic level.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why only approximately 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is available to the next trophic level.
rubric.minimum_fix: About 90 percent of energy is lost as heat through cellular respiration and metabolic processes at each trophic level; only about 10 percent is stored in new biomass available to the next level.

accepted_variants: less energy to frogs then to hawks
rubric.evidence_requirements: Hawk population would decrease. Fewer grasshoppers means less energy available to frogs (the trophic level below hawks); frog population declines; less energy available to hawks; hawk birth rate falls and/or death rate rises; hawk population shrinks. Loss of energy at one trophic level cascades up the food chain.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how the hawk population would be affected if the grasshopper population declined sharply, and explain using energy flow principles.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fewer grasshoppers reduces energy available to frogs; frog population declines; reduced frog population provides less energy to hawks; hawk population decreases due to reduced food supply.

items.stem: Ecologists studying a meadow ecosystem measure biomass and energy at each trophic level of the food chain: grass to grasshopper to frog to hawk.
items.stimulus: A pyramid of energy shows: grass 10,000 kcal, grasshoppers 1,000 kcal, frogs 100 kcal, hawks 10 kcal.

accepted_variants: gap junctions: connexin proteins, no cell wall
rubric.evidence_requirements: Gap junctions: protein channels (connexins) span both plasma membranes of adjacent animal cells, forming a direct cytoplasmic connection; no cell wall involved. Plasmodesmata: channels lined with plasma membrane that pass through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting cytoplasm; may contain desmotubule (ER strand).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare the structure of gap junctions in animal cells to plasmodesmata in plant cells.
rubric.minimum_fix: Gap junctions are protein-lined channels through adjacent animal cell plasma membranes; plasmodesmata are channels through plant cell walls lined with plasma membrane, directly connecting plant cell cytoplasm.

accepted_variants: action potential propagates cell to cell
rubric.evidence_requirements: Gap junctions allow ions (Na+, Ca2+, K+) and small molecules to pass directly between cardiac muscle cells; an electrical signal (action potential) depolarizes one cell and ions flow through gap junctions to the next cell, triggering its depolarization; the signal propagates cell-to-cell as a wave without requiring neuromuscular junctions at each cell.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how gap junctions allow cardiac muscle cells to contract in a coordinated wave.
rubric.minimum_fix: Gap junctions allow ions to pass directly between cardiac muscle cells; an electrical signal in one cell spreads to adjacent cells through gap junctions, causing coordinated depolarization and contraction across the heart tissue.

items.stem: Cells in multicellular organisms communicate and exchange materials through direct cell-to-cell connections.
items.stimulus: A diagram shows two animal cells joined by gap junctions (connexin channels) and two plant cells joined by plasmodesmata passing through the cell wall.

accepted_variants: inner membrane resembles bacterial plasma membrane
rubric.evidence_requirements: Any two of: (1) mitochondria have their own circular DNA, resembling prokaryotic chromosomes; (2) mitochondria have 70S ribosomes similar to bacteria, not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (3) mitochondria reproduce by binary fission; (4) mitochondria have inner membranes similar in composition to bacterial plasma membranes; (5) mitochondria are similar in size to bacteria.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe two pieces of evidence from mitochondria that support the endosymbiotic theory.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA similar to bacterial chromosomes; mitochondria have 70S ribosomes like bacteria, not the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm.

accepted_variants: outer membrane from host cell endocytosis
inner membrane from prokaryote plasma membrane
two membranes from two different origins
rubric.evidence_requirements: The outer membrane is derived from the host cell membrane that surrounded the engulfed prokaryote during endocytosis; the inner membrane is derived from the original prokaryotic plasma membrane. Two separate membrane origins produce the double-membrane structure.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the double membrane of the mitochondrion is consistent with the endosymbiotic theory.
rubric.minimum_fix: The outer mitochondrial membrane came from the host cell plasma membrane when the prokaryote was engulfed; the inner membrane is the remnant of the original prokaryotic plasma membrane — two distinct origins explain the double membrane.

items.stem: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell and eventually became permanent organelles.
items.stimulus: No additional stimulus provided. Students answer based on knowledge of mitochondrial structure, genetics, and biochemistry.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Blood glucose rises above set point; pancreatic beta cells detect elevated glucose; insulin is secreted; insulin stimulates muscle and adipose cells to take up glucose and liver to store glucose as glycogen; blood glucose falls back to set point; falling glucose reduces insulin secretion, completing the negative feedback loop.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how a negative feedback loop returns blood glucose to the set point after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
rubric.minimum_fix: Rising blood glucose triggers insulin secretion from beta cells; insulin signals cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen; blood glucose returns to set point; reduced glucose lowers insulin release.

accepted_variants: positive feedback drives process to completion
adaptive because completes a rapid necessary event
rubric.evidence_requirements: Any valid example: (1) childbirth — oxytocin promotes uterine contractions; stronger contractions release more oxytocin; cycle escalates until baby is delivered, then stops (adaptive: ensures delivery is completed quickly); (2) blood clotting — platelets activate more platelets to rapidly seal a wound; (3) action potential depolarization — Na+ influx opens more Na+ channels. In each case the amplification drives a specific process to rapid completion, which is beneficial.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify one example of positive feedback in human physiology and explain why it is adaptive despite amplifying a deviation from a baseline.
rubric.minimum_fix: During childbirth, oxytocin promotes uterine contractions; contractions stimulate more oxytocin release, amplifying contractions until delivery — positive feedback is adaptive because it drives labor to completion quickly rather than stalling.

items.stem: The human body maintains blood glucose concentration within a narrow range through hormonal feedback mechanisms.
items.stimulus: A graph shows blood glucose rising after a carbohydrate-rich meal, then returning to the set point over approximately 2 hours.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that a peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water (dehydration synthesis).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how two amino acids are joined and identify the bond formed.
rubric.minimum_fix: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl and amino groups of adjacent amino acids, releasing a water molecule.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Identifies the long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail that cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how the structure of a fatty acid makes it hydrophobic.
rubric.minimum_fix: The long nonpolar hydrocarbon chain cannot interact with polar water molecules, making the fatty acid hydrophobic.

items.stem: A student compares the structures of an amino acid, a monosaccharide, and a fatty acid to determine which macromolecule each monomer builds.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that both inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site; a higher substrate concentration statistically outcompetes the inhibitor.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why increasing substrate concentration can overcome competitive inhibition.
rubric.minimum_fix: More substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for binding to the active site, restoring normal enzyme function.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that a noncompetitive inhibitor binds a different (allosteric) site, changing the active site shape so substrate cannot bind regardless of its concentration.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the same strategy would NOT work against a noncompetitive inhibitor.
rubric.minimum_fix: The noncompetitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site, altering the active site shape so more substrate cannot overcome the inhibition.

items.stem: A researcher adds a molecule that resembles the substrate of an enzyme and observes that increasing substrate concentration eventually restores enzyme activity.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that the acidic environment maintains the ionic and hydrogen bonds that shape pepsin's active site.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why pepsin functions optimally at pH 2.
rubric.minimum_fix: At pH 2, the ionic interactions that maintain pepsin's active site conformation are optimized for substrate binding.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States trypsin activity decreases or ceases because low pH disrupts bonds maintaining the active site, causing denaturation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict and explain what happens to trypsin activity at pH 2.
rubric.minimum_fix: Low pH disrupts hydrogen and ionic bonds in trypsin's structure, denaturing the active site and eliminating activity.

items.stem: An experiment measures enzyme activity at pH 2, 7, and 11 for two digestive enzymes: pepsin (stomach) and trypsin (small intestine).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name two: (1) can form 4 covalent bonds; (2) can bond to other carbons to form long chains or rings.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain two properties of carbon that allow it to form the diverse molecules found in living organisms.
rubric.minimum_fix: Carbon forms 4 stable covalent bonds and can bond to other carbons, producing long chains, branches, and ring structures.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that a hydroxyl group makes the compound polar and able to form hydrogen bonds with water (increasing solubility).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a hydroxyl group (-OH) changes the chemical behavior of a carbon compound.
rubric.minimum_fix: A hydroxyl group is polar and can form hydrogen bonds with water, making the molecule more water-soluble.

items.stem: A biologist notes that carbon forms the backbone of all organic molecules and investigates carbon's bonding properties.

accepted_variants: hydrogen bonds require energy to break
rubric.evidence_requirements: States that breaking hydrogen bonds requires energy; water absorbs much heat before temperature rises, stabilizing temperatures.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how hydrogen bonding between water molecules gives water its high specific heat capacity.
rubric.minimum_fix: Water must absorb a large amount of heat to break hydrogen bonds before temperature rises, stabilizing aquatic and cellular temperatures.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that polar water molecules surround ions, separating them; positive ends attract Cl and negative ends attract Na.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why water is an excellent solvent for ionic compounds such as NaCl.
rubric.minimum_fix: Polar water molecules surround and separate Na+ and Cl- ions, keeping them dissolved in solution.

items.stem: Students investigate the unique properties of water and how those properties support life.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Identifies any two of: nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplast, ER, Golgi, vacuole; explains function of one correctly.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify two structures present in the plant cell but absent in the bacterial cell and explain the function of one.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mitochondria and a nucleus are present in plant cells but not bacteria; the nucleus houses DNA for gene regulation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that lacking organelles reduces energy and material cost; simpler cell allows faster replication.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain one advantage prokaryotes gain from lacking membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without the overhead of producing organelles, prokaryotes can replicate faster and use fewer resources.

items.stem: A researcher compares a bacterial cell to a plant cell under an electron microscope.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name: ribosome to rough ER to Golgi to secretory vesicle to plasma membrane (exocytosis); at least 3 correct in order.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the path of the secretory protein from synthesis to secretion, naming the organelles in order.
rubric.minimum_fix: The protein is made on rough ER ribosomes, enters the ER lumen, moves to the Golgi for modification, then exits by exocytosis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that the Golgi modifies (e.g., glycosylation), sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles for the correct destination.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of the Golgi apparatus in processing the secretory protein.
rubric.minimum_fix: The Golgi modifies the protein (such as adding carbohydrates) and sorts it into vesicles directed to the plasma membrane.

items.stem: A cell synthesizes a secretory protein. The protein begins on ribosomes and must reach the extracellular space.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name two of: double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission, similar size to bacteria.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify two pieces of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, both features consistent with a prokaryotic ancestor.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the outer membrane came from the host cell's engulfment vesicle; the inner membrane is the original bacterial membrane.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the double membrane of mitochondria is consistent with the endosymbiotic theory.
rubric.minimum_fix: The outer membrane is derived from the host's engulfment vesicle, while the inner membrane is the original bacterial plasma membrane.

items.stem: Scientists propose that mitochondria evolved from an ancient aerobic bacterium engulfed by a larger cell (endosymbiotic theory).

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the cell loses water by osmosis (water moves to higher solute outside); describes the vacuole shrinking and plasmolysis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe what happens to the plant cell in the concentrated salt solution and explain the mechanism.
rubric.minimum_fix: Water exits by osmosis to the hypertonic salt solution, the central vacuole shrinks, and the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the cell wall resists expansion; as turgor pressure builds against the wall, it prevents further water intake.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a plant cell does not burst when placed in a hypotonic (dilute) solution.
rubric.minimum_fix: The rigid cell wall resists swelling; as water enters and turgor pressure increases, the wall pushes back, preventing bursting.

items.stem: A plant cell is placed in a highly concentrated salt solution.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in; creates electrochemical gradient with negative interior.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how the sodium-potassium pump maintains the resting membrane potential of a neuron.
rubric.minimum_fix: The pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed, creating a negative interior charge and ion gradients.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States membrane potential collapses toward zero (depolarizes) because Na+ leaks in and gradients dissipate without active pumping.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what happens to the membrane potential if the pump is blocked and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without the pump, Na+ leaks into the cell and the ion gradients dissipate, causing the membrane to depolarize.

items.stem: A researcher adds a substance that blocks the sodium-potassium pump in nerve cells.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the double bond creates a kink in the tail, preventing tight packing of phospholipids, so the membrane remains fluid.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why unsaturated fatty acids increase membrane fluidity.
rubric.minimum_fix: The double bond bends the hydrocarbon tail, preventing phospholipids from packing tightly, which increases membrane fluidity.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States cholesterol stabilizes fluidity: restricts movement at high temp (prevents too fluid) and prevents packing at low temp (prevents solidifying).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of cholesterol in maintaining membrane fluidity across a range of temperatures.
rubric.minimum_fix: Cholesterol reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents solidification at low temperatures, acting as a fluidity buffer.

items.stem: A student observes that membrane fluidity increases when unsaturated fatty acids replace saturated fatty acids in phospholipids.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States glucose is large and polar; the hydrophobic bilayer interior repels polar molecules.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why glucose cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion.
rubric.minimum_fix: Glucose is too large and polar to cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer without assistance.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States facilitated diffusion moves molecules down their gradient without ATP; active transport moves molecules against gradient and requires ATP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe one way facilitated diffusion differs from active transport.
rubric.minimum_fix: Facilitated diffusion does not require ATP and moves molecules down their gradient, while active transport uses ATP to move molecules against the gradient.

items.stem: Cells take up glucose via facilitated diffusion using glucose transporter (GLUT) proteins, even though glucose is a large polar molecule.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include: ligand binds receptor, membrane invaginates, vesicle pinches off into cytoplasm.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the steps by which a cell takes up a molecule via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
rubric.minimum_fix: The ligand binds to receptors clustered in a coated pit; the membrane invaginates and a vesicle pinches off into the cytoplasm.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that only molecules that bind specific cell-surface receptors are taken up, providing selectivity.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how receptor-mediated endocytosis allows a cell to take up specific molecules selectively.
rubric.minimum_fix: Only molecules that match the shape of the cell-surface receptor are taken up, giving the cell control over what enters.

items.stem: A researcher studies how the influenza virus enters host cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States RuBisCO catalyzes the attachment of CO2 to RuBP (5-carbon), producing two molecules of 3-PGA (3-carbon).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the role of RuBisCO in carbon fixation during the Calvin cycle.
rubric.minimum_fix: RuBisCO attaches CO2 to the 5-carbon RuBP, producing two 3-carbon 3-PGA molecules as the first stable product.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the Calvin cycle requires ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions; without them CO2 cannot be fixed and RuBP cannot be regenerated.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the Calvin cycle would stop if the light reactions were blocked.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without light reactions there is no ATP or NADPH; CO2 cannot be reduced to G3P and RuBP cannot be regenerated.

items.stem: After the light reactions produce ATP and NADPH, a Calvin cycle enzyme fixes CO2 into organic molecules in the stroma.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States PEP carboxylase has a higher affinity for CO2 and cannot fix O2, so photorespiration is avoided.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the advantage of using PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells instead of RuBisCO.
rubric.minimum_fix: PEP carboxylase does not react with O2 and has higher CO2 affinity than RuBisCO, preventing wasteful photorespiration.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that high local CO2 concentration saturates RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells, maximizing Calvin cycle efficiency and suppressing photorespiration.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe why concentrating CO2 in bundle-sheath cells benefits photosynthesis in C4 plants.
rubric.minimum_fix: High CO2 in bundle-sheath cells keeps RuBisCO active in the Calvin cycle and prevents it from reacting with O2.

items.stem: C4 plants such as corn use a two-stage carbon fixation process to minimize photorespiration in hot, dry conditions.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States aerobic respiration uses the ETC and chemiosmosis to generate ~30 ATP from NADH/FADH2; fermentation only produces 2 ATP from glycolysis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why aerobic respiration produces far more ATP per glucose than fermentation.
rubric.minimum_fix: Aerobic respiration passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 through the ETC to make ~30 ATP; fermentation only produces 2 ATP in glycolysis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fermentation regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate, allowing glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the metabolic role of fermentation in allowing continued ATP production when oxygen is absent.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fermentation oxidizes NADH back to NAD+ using pyruvate as the electron acceptor, which allows glycolysis to keep running.

items.stem: A student compares ATP production in aerobic respiration versus fermentation in yeast under different oxygen conditions.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name: 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP; explains NADH/FADH2 carry electrons to ETC.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the products of one turn of the Krebs cycle and state the significance of NADH and FADH2.
rubric.minimum_fix: One turn produces 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP; the NADH and FADH2 carry electrons to the ETC for more ATP.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that glycolysis breaks glucose into two pyruvate molecules, each yielding one acetyl-CoA, so the cycle runs once per acetyl-CoA.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the Krebs cycle must turn twice for each glucose molecule.
rubric.minimum_fix: Glucose produces two pyruvate molecules, each converted to one acetyl-CoA, so the cycle must turn twice per glucose.

items.stem: During the Krebs cycle, acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to begin a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States protons flow down their gradient through ATP synthase, releasing energy used to phosphorylate ADP to ATP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how ATP synthase normally produces ATP during cellular respiration.
rubric.minimum_fix: Protons flow from the intermembrane space through ATP synthase into the matrix, and the energy released phosphorylates ADP to ATP.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States ATP levels drop dramatically because oxidative phosphorylation stops; only glycolysis and Krebs substrate-level phosphorylation remain (2-4 ATP total per glucose).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what happens to cellular ATP levels when ATP synthase is blocked, and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Blocking ATP synthase stops chemiosmosis; only the 4 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation remain, causing severe ATP depletion.

items.stem: A toxin blocks ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane of liver cells.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include: ligand binds GPCR, G-protein activated, adenylyl cyclase activated, ATP to cAMP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the signal transduction pathway from epinephrine binding to cAMP production.
rubric.minimum_fix: Epinephrine binds the GPCR, activating the G-protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase to convert ATP to cAMP.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States cAMP amplifies the signal (one hormone activates many cAMP molecules) and relays the signal inside the cell without the hormone entering.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the advantage of using a second messenger like cAMP in signal transduction.
rubric.minimum_fix: cAMP amplifies the signal: one epinephrine molecule activates many G-proteins, each producing many cAMP molecules.

items.stem: Epinephrine binds to a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) on liver cells and triggers glycogen breakdown.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States: dimerization of two RTKs, autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues, docking of relay proteins.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the molecular events that occur when a growth factor binds to its RTK.
rubric.minimum_fix: Ligand binding causes two RTK monomers to dimerize; each phosphorylates the other's tyrosines, creating docking sites for relay proteins.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States permanently active RTK sends continuous growth signals even without growth factor, driving uncontrolled cell division.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a mutation that keeps RTK permanently active could lead to cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: A constitutively active RTK continuously signals cell division without growth factor, bypassing normal controls and causing cancer.

items.stem: A growth factor binds to a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) on the surface of a dividing cell.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States apoptosis sculpts tissues (e.g., finger separation), eliminates self-reactive immune cells, and removes cells with damaged DNA.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the biological importance of apoptosis during normal development.
rubric.minimum_fix: Apoptosis removes cells with DNA damage, sculpts developing tissues such as separating fingers, and eliminates excess cells.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States apoptosis is orderly and packaged into apoptotic bodies taken up by phagocytes (no inflammation); necrosis causes cell lysis and triggers inflammation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguish apoptosis from necrosis in terms of cellular effects on surrounding tissue.
rubric.minimum_fix: Apoptosis packages cell contents into vesicles for phagocytosis without inflammation; necrosis lyses the cell, releasing contents that cause inflammation.

items.stem: A cell receives a signal that triggers apoptosis. Caspase enzymes are activated and the cell dismantles itself.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the G1 checkpoint ensures DNA is undamaged before replication; damaged cells are held or undergo apoptosis, preventing mutation propagation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of the G1 checkpoint in preventing cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: The G1 checkpoint prevents cells with damaged DNA from copying the damage into daughter cells, reducing the risk of cancer.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States cyclins bind CDKs; cyclin levels fluctuate through the cycle; cyclin-CDK complexes phosphorylate target proteins that advance the cycle.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how cyclin-CDK complexes control passage through the cell cycle checkpoints.
rubric.minimum_fix: Cyclins accumulate and bind CDKs; the active complex phosphorylates proteins that drive the cell through checkpoints.

items.stem: Researchers study the cell cycle and find that a specific checkpoint prevents cells with damaged DNA from entering S phase.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must include: action potential arrives, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ enters, vesicles fuse, neurotransmitter released.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the sequence of events that leads to neurotransmitter release at a chemical synapse.
rubric.minimum_fix: An action potential reaches the terminal, opens Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ influx causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States EPSP depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane (excitatory, more likely to fire); IPSP hyperpolarizes it (inhibitory, less likely to fire).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the difference between an EPSP and an IPSP at the postsynaptic neuron.
rubric.minimum_fix: An EPSP depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane, increasing the chance of an action potential; an IPSP hyperpolarizes it, reducing that chance.

items.stem: Neurons communicate across a synapse when an action potential arrives at the axon terminal.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States auxin moves to the shaded side; cells on that side elongate more than cells on the lit side, bending the stem toward light.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how unequal auxin distribution causes a plant stem to bend toward light.
rubric.minimum_fix: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, promoting greater cell elongation there, so the stem bends toward the light source.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States auxin activates proton pumps; lowered pH activates wall-loosening enzymes (expansins), allowing cells to expand as they take in water.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the mechanism by which auxin promotes cell elongation in stem cells.
rubric.minimum_fix: Auxin activates proton pumps that lower cell wall pH, activating expansins that loosen wall cross-links so cells can elongate.

items.stem: A plant stem bends toward a light source in a response known as phototropism.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States 9 yellow round : 3 yellow wrinkled : 3 green round : 1 green wrinkled; explains independent assortment.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict the phenotypic ratio of offspring from the YyRr x YyRr cross and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Independent assortment of the two genes produces a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16; must show multiplication of individual probabilities.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate the probability of producing a plant that is homozygous dominant for both traits.
rubric.minimum_fix: The probability of YYRR is (1/4)(1/4) = 1/16, applying the product rule for independent events.

items.stem: In peas, yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y) and round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). Two dihybrid plants (YyRr x YyRr) are crossed.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States sons get X from mother (50% X^b) and Y from father; therefore 50% (1/2) of sons are color blind.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict the probability that a son of this couple will be color blind. Show your work.
rubric.minimum_fix: Sons inherit one X from their carrier mother; half carry X^b, so 1/2 of sons are color blind.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States daughters receive X^B from the father; they can be at most carriers (X^B X^b) but never homozygous recessive.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why daughters of this couple cannot be color blind.
rubric.minimum_fix: Daughters always receive the normal X^B allele from their father; they cannot be X^b X^b, so none are color blind.

items.stem: Red-green color blindness is an X-linked recessive trait. A carrier woman (X^B X^b) has children with a man who has normal vision (X^B Y).

rubric.evidence_requirements: States neither allele completely masks the other; heterozygote produces intermediate amount of red pigment, resulting in pink.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the heterozygous (RW) snapdragon has pink flowers rather than red or white.
rubric.minimum_fix: With incomplete dominance, the RW plant produces less red pigment than RR, resulting in a pink intermediate phenotype.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States RW x RW gives 1 RR (red) : 2 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white), a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict the phenotypic ratio of a cross between two pink snapdragons and explain your reasoning.
rubric.minimum_fix: RW x RW gives 1/4 RR (red), 2/4 RW (pink), 1/4 WW (white) — a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.

items.stem: In snapdragons, red flower (R) and white flower (W) alleles show incomplete dominance; heterozygotes (RW) are pink.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States codominance = both alleles fully expressed (type AB has both A and B antigens); incomplete dominance = intermediate phenotype.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how codominance differs from incomplete dominance, using blood type as an example.
rubric.minimum_fix: In codominance (AB blood type) both antigens are fully present; in incomplete dominance neither allele is fully expressed and an intermediate results.

accepted_variants: I^A I^B, I^A i, I^B i, ii
rubric.evidence_requirements: Lists: I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), ii (O) — all four blood types possible.
rubric.learner_facing_text: A type A parent (I^A i) and a type B parent (I^B i) have children. Identify all possible blood types of their offspring.
rubric.minimum_fix: Their cross (I^A i x I^B i) can produce I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), and ii (O).

items.stem: Human ABO blood type is controlled by three alleles (I^A, I^B, i). I^A and I^B are codominant; i is recessive to both.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States that one E allele is sufficient to allow pigment expression; Bb with E present gives black coat.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a dog that is BbEe is black rather than yellow.
rubric.minimum_fix: Because the dog has at least one E allele, pigment is expressed; Bb produces black color.

rubric.evidence_requirements: BbEe x bbee: offspring are Bb or bb (1:1) and Ee or ee (1:1). Half are ee = yellow. Answer: 1/2.
rubric.learner_facing_text: A BbEe dog is crossed with a bbee dog. What fraction of offspring will be yellow?
rubric.minimum_fix: BbEe x bbee gives 1/2 Ee and 1/2 ee offspring; only ee dogs are yellow, so 1/2 are yellow.

items.stem: Two genes control coat color in Labrador retrievers: B (black vs. brown) and E (expression vs. no expression of pigment). The ee genotype blocks all pigment.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States linked genes are on the same chromosome; they travel together during meiosis unless crossing over occurs.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why linked genes do not follow Mendel's law of independent assortment.
rubric.minimum_fix: Linked genes are on the same chromosome and move together during meiosis, violating independent assortment.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States homologous chromosomes exchange segments during prophase I; crossing over between the two genes creates new allele combinations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how crossing over can produce recombinant offspring from two linked genes.
rubric.minimum_fix: During prophase I, homologs exchange segments at chiasmata; if the crossover occurs between two linked genes, new allele combinations are produced.

items.stem: A biologist finds that two genes on the same chromosome are inherited together more often than expected by independent assortment.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States both homologs go to same cell; two gametes get 2 copies of the chromosome; two get 0 copies (n+1 and n-1).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe what happens to chromosome number in the gametes when nondisjunction occurs at meiosis I.
rubric.minimum_fix: Nondisjunction at meiosis I causes both homologs to enter the same cell, producing n+1 and n-1 gametes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States chromosome 21 is the smallest autosome with fewest genes; triplication of larger chromosomes disrupts too many genes to be viable.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why trisomy 21 is survivable but most other trisomies are lethal in early development.
rubric.minimum_fix: Chromosome 21 has very few genes, so having three copies is tolerated; most other autosomes have more genes, making trisomy lethal.

items.stem: A human cell undergoing meiosis fails to separate homologous chromosomes during meiosis I.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transcription factors bind the TATA box/promoter; RNA polymerase is recruited and unwinds the DNA to begin synthesis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how RNA polymerase initiates transcription at a eukaryotic promoter.
rubric.minimum_fix: Transcription factors bind the promoter (TATA box); RNA polymerase is recruited to the complex and unwinds DNA to start RNA synthesis.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States both protect mRNA from degradation and the 5' cap assists ribosome binding; the poly-A tail also aids nuclear export.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the purpose of the 5' cap and poly-A tail added to eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
rubric.minimum_fix: The 5' cap protects mRNA from exonucleases and assists ribosome binding; the poly-A tail stabilizes the mRNA and aids export.

items.stem: RNA polymerase binds to a promoter on the DNA template strand and synthesizes a pre-mRNA molecule.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States A site holds incoming aminoacyl-tRNA; P site holds growing polypeptide chain; peptide bond forms transferring chain to A site.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the roles of the A site and P site during elongation of a polypeptide chain.
rubric.minimum_fix: The A site accepts the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA; peptidyl transferase forms a bond transferring the growing chain from the P site to the new amino acid.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States alternative splicing allows different exons to be included or excluded, producing different mRNAs and proteins from the same pre-mRNA.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a single gene can produce multiple protein isoforms in eukaryotes.
rubric.minimum_fix: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons, generating multiple mRNAs and protein isoforms from one gene.

items.stem: A ribosome translates an mRNA sequence starting from the start codon AUG.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States methyl groups on cytosines block transcription factor binding or recruit proteins that compact chromatin, silencing the gene.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how DNA methylation can silence gene expression.
rubric.minimum_fix: Methylation of cytosines in a promoter blocks transcription factor binding, preventing RNA polymerase from initiating transcription.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States acetylation neutralizes positive histone charge, loosening interaction with negatively charged DNA; chromatin opens and transcription factors access the gene.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how histone acetylation increases gene expression.
rubric.minimum_fix: Histone acetylation reduces the positive charge on histones, loosening chromatin structure and allowing transcription factors to access the DNA.

items.stem: Scientists observe that gene expression in a developing embryo can be altered by DNA methylation without changing the DNA sequence.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States DNA loops bring the enhancer near the promoter; activator bound to enhancer contacts transcription machinery at the promoter.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how an enhancer located far from a gene can increase that gene's transcription.
rubric.minimum_fix: The DNA between the enhancer and promoter loops so that activator proteins bound to the enhancer can contact and recruit RNA polymerase.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transcription would decrease or stop because the activator cannot contact the promoter and recruit RNA polymerase.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to gene expression if the activator protein that binds this enhancer were mutated and could no longer bind DNA.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without activator binding, the enhancer cannot recruit RNA polymerase to the promoter, and gene expression would drop significantly.

items.stem: A cell produces large amounts of a protein in response to an environmental signal; a researcher finds this involves an enhancer element far from the gene's promoter.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States miRNA base-pairs with complementary sequence in target mRNA's 3' UTR; RISC complex either blocks translation or cleaves the mRNA.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism by which a miRNA silences its target mRNA.
rubric.minimum_fix: The miRNA base-pairs with the target mRNA's 3' UTR in the RISC complex, blocking ribosome access or triggering mRNA cleavage.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States if miRNA can no longer bind the proto-oncogene mRNA, the gene is overexpressed; uncontrolled growth factor production could drive cancer.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why mutations in miRNA target sites in a proto-oncogene could contribute to cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without miRNA silencing, the proto-oncogene is overexpressed, producing excess growth-promoting protein and potentially driving cancer.

items.stem: microRNAs (miRNAs) are short non-coding RNA molecules that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States directional selection; justification: one extreme phenotype (light fur) is favored, shifting the population mean.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the type of natural selection acting on this mouse population and justify your answer.
rubric.minimum_fix: Directional selection is occurring because one extreme (light fur) provides camouflage, increasing survival and shifting the population.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States genetic drift causes random changes in allele frequency due to chance, which may reinforce or oppose selection; in small populations drift can overpower selection.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how this population can evolve if random genetic drift also acts on it.
rubric.minimum_fix: Genetic drift causes random allele frequency changes; in small populations it can speed up or reverse the shift caused by natural selection.

items.stem: A population of mice lives on light-colored sand dunes. Over generations, the average fur color shifts from dark to light.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the bottleneck drastically reduces population size; allele frequencies shift by chance; rare alleles may be lost and common alleles overrepresented.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the bottleneck effect and its impact on genetic diversity.
rubric.minimum_fix: A bottleneck reduces the gene pool to a few survivors; alleles are lost by chance, reducing genetic diversity in the rebounded population.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States with less variation, individuals are more genetically similar; if a new disease or environmental change occurs, most individuals may be susceptible.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a loss of genetic diversity could be harmful to the butterfly population's long-term survival.
rubric.minimum_fix: Low genetic diversity means fewer individuals carry alleles for disease resistance or other adaptations, making the population vulnerable to new threats.

items.stem: A large population of butterflies is reduced to 20 individuals after a disease outbreak; the survivors repopulate the island.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States females preferentially mate with elaborate-tailed males; these males have greater reproductive success, passing the trait to more offspring.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how sexual selection can maintain an energetically costly trait like the peacock tail.
rubric.minimum_fix: Females choose elaborate-tailed males; those males sire more offspring, so the alleles for the tail increase in frequency despite survival costs.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States increased predation on long-tailed males would select against the trait; natural selection would reduce average tail length over generations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how peacock tail length would change if a new predator preferentially targeted long-tailed males.
rubric.minimum_fix: Predation on long-tailed males would increase selection against the trait, shifting the population toward shorter tails over generations.

items.stem: Male peacocks with longer, more colorful tails are preferred by females, even though the tail is energetically costly and increases predation risk.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States cytochrome c accumulates mutations at a roughly constant rate; more differences = more time since common ancestor.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why cytochrome c sequence differences can be used to estimate the time of divergence between species.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mutations in cytochrome c accumulate over time; comparing the number of differences gives an estimate of time since two species diverged.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States humans and chimpanzees share a more recent common ancestor than humans and horses; they diverged more recently.
rubric.learner_facing_text: If humans and chimpanzees differ by 0 amino acids in cytochrome c and humans and horses differ by 12, what can you conclude?
rubric.minimum_fix: Humans and chimpanzees have identical cytochrome c, indicating very recent common ancestry; 12 differences with horses indicate much earlier divergence.

items.stem: Scientists compare DNA sequences of cytochrome c in humans, chimpanzees, and horses to determine evolutionary relationships.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States geographic barrier prevents gene flow; populations accumulate different mutations and adaptations; diverge genetically until reproductively isolated.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how allopatric speciation leads to the formation of two species from one ancestral population.
rubric.minimum_fix: A geographic barrier stops gene flow; each population independently evolves until they are so different they can no longer produce viable offspring.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States any prezygotic mechanism (different mating calls, timing, habitat preference) or postzygotic (hybrid inviability, sterility).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain one mechanism of reproductive isolation that could keep the two finch populations from interbreeding if the barrier is removed.
rubric.minimum_fix: Behavioral isolation: if the populations evolved different mating calls, females would reject males from the other population.

items.stem: A population of finches on a large island diverges into two populations that differ in beak size after a geographic barrier forms.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States resistance alleles already existed before antibiotic exposure; antibiotic selected FOR pre-existing resistant individuals, not inducing resistance.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how natural selection accounts for the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance without invoking Lamarckian inheritance.
rubric.minimum_fix: Resistance alleles were already present in some bacteria before antibiotic exposure; the antibiotic killed sensitive bacteria and resistant ones reproduced.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States stopping early leaves partially resistant bacteria alive; these survive and reproduce, passing moderate-resistance alleles on, selecting for more resistant strains.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why using antibiotics incorrectly (stopping the course early) can accelerate resistance evolution.
rubric.minimum_fix: Stopping early leaves bacteria with partial resistance alive; those survivors reproduce and face further selection, driving resistance to higher levels.

items.stem: A population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic. Within 10 generations, most bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States remaining 90% is lost as heat during cellular respiration, used for movement, or is undigested and passes as waste.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next.
rubric.minimum_fix: About 90% of energy is lost as metabolic heat and waste; only 10% is stored in biomass available to the next level.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States hawk (10 kJ) needs 100 kJ from birds, which needs 1000 kJ from caterpillars, which needs 10,000 kJ from plants.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Using the 10% rule, calculate how much plant energy (in kJ) must be produced to support a hawk that needs 10 kJ.
rubric.minimum_fix: 10 kJ hawk / 0.1 = 100 kJ birds / 0.1 = 1000 kJ caterpillars / 0.1 = 10,000 kJ plants.

items.stem: A forest food web includes plants, caterpillars, birds, and a hawk. A student calculates that only 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States: excess nitrogen causes algal bloom; algae die; decomposers respire; O2 depleted; fish and other organisms die.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the process of eutrophication and how it leads to a dead zone in the pond.
rubric.minimum_fix: Excess nitrogen fuels an algal bloom; dead algae are decomposed by bacteria that consume oxygen, creating a hypoxic dead zone.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States algae are primary producers (trophic level 1); they fix solar energy into organic matter via photosynthesis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the trophic level of the algae in this scenario and explain its role as a primary producer.
rubric.minimum_fix: Algae are primary producers — they convert light energy into organic molecules via photosynthesis, forming the base of the food web.

items.stem: Scientists monitor nitrogen levels in a pond and find that excess agricultural runoff causes a bloom of algae followed by a dead zone.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States primary succession starts from bare, lifeless substrate (no soil); secondary succession begins after disturbance of existing community (soil remains). Lava island = primary.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguish between primary and secondary succession and identify the type occurring on the lava island.
rubric.minimum_fix: Primary succession starts with no soil on bare substrate; secondary begins where soil already exists. The lava island undergoes primary succession.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States pioneers modify the environment: they break down rock, fix nitrogen, add organic matter, building soil that other species require.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of pioneer species in enabling later successional stages.
rubric.minimum_fix: Pioneers weathering rock and adding organic matter as they die creates soil, allowing less tolerant but more competitive species to colonize.

items.stem: A volcano destroys all life on a newly formed lava island. Over decades, pioneer species begin to colonize the bare rock.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States keystone species has a disproportionately large effect; removing otters causes urchin population to explode, kelp devoured, ecosystem collapses.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain what a keystone species is and describe the trophic cascade caused by the loss of sea otters.
rubric.minimum_fix: A keystone species has outsized ecosystem impact; without otters, urchins overgraze kelp, collapsing the kelp forest ecosystem.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States otter restoration suppresses urchins, kelp recovers, more species supported by kelp habitat, species richness increases.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict one way restoring the sea otter population would affect species richness in the ecosystem.
rubric.minimum_fix: Restored otter populations suppress urchins, allowing kelp to recover and provide habitat for many species, increasing species richness.

items.stem: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp. When otters were hunted to near extinction, kelp forests disappeared.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States density-dependent limiting factors (food, disease, predation) intensify as population grows, reducing per capita reproductive success.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why population growth rate slows as the rabbit population approaches carrying capacity.
rubric.minimum_fix: As rabbits approach K, food becomes scarce and disease spreads more easily; birth rates fall and death rates rise, slowing growth.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States r-selected = many offspring, little parental care, short lifespan, rapid maturity (rabbits); K-selected = fewer offspring, more care, longer lifespan.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguish between r-selected and K-selected life history strategies using rabbits as an example of an r-selected species.
rubric.minimum_fix: Rabbits are r-selected: they reproduce rapidly with many offspring and little parental investment; K-selected species invest more in fewer offspring.

items.stem: A population ecologist tracks a population of rabbits and finds that the growth rate declines as the population approaches carrying capacity (K).

rubric.evidence_requirements: States commensalism (+/0); clownfish benefits from protection, anemone is neither helped nor harmed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify the relationship between clownfish and sea anemone and justify your answer.
rubric.minimum_fix: This is commensalism: the clownfish benefits by living safely in the anemone's tentacles, and the anemone is unaffected.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Names a valid mutualism (bees and flowers, mycorrhizae and plants, N-fixing bacteria and legumes); states both species benefit in mutualism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe one example of mutualism and explain how it differs from commensalism.
rubric.minimum_fix: Mycorrhizal fungi extend plant root absorption and receive carbohydrates in return — both benefit, unlike commensalism where only one does.

items.stem: Clownfish live within the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. The fish are protected from predators; the anemone receives no clear benefit.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States larger islands have more diverse habitats and larger population sizes per species, reducing local extinction risk.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why larger islands tend to support more species than smaller islands of equal distance from the mainland.
rubric.minimum_fix: Larger islands offer more habitat types and support bigger populations, reducing extinction rates and allowing more species to coexist.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States species richness would decrease because immigration rate drops with distance; fewer species colonize successfully.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how species richness on an island would change if the distance from the mainland doubled, and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Doubling the distance reduces the immigration rate because fewer colonizers reach the island; this lowers species richness at equilibrium.

items.stem: Scientists compare species richness on large islands and small islands of equal distance from the mainland.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States more moose gives more food for wolves, wolf population increases, more predation reduces moose, wolves decline, moose recover, cycle repeats.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism that generates the cyclical fluctuations in wolf and moose populations.
rubric.minimum_fix: As moose increase, wolves have more food and multiply; more wolves reduce moose; fewer moose starve wolves; wolf decline allows moose recovery.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States moose would increase rapidly without predation pressure, likely overshoot K, and then decline due to overgrazing or starvation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to the moose population if all wolves were removed from the island.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without wolves, moose would increase unchecked, overshoot carrying capacity, overgraze vegetation, and then crash due to starvation.

items.stem: A field ecologist studies a predator-prey relationship between wolves and moose on an island, recording population cycles over 50 years.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States water moves from soil (less negative water potential) into the plant cell (more negative water potential) by osmosis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain in which direction water will move between the plant cell and the soil solution, and why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Water moves from the soil (higher water potential) into the cell (lower, more negative water potential) by osmosis down the gradient.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States as water enters, turgor pressure increases; this raises water potential of the cell, reducing the gradient and slowing water uptake until equilibrium.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how turgor pressure changes as water enters the plant cell and its effect on water uptake.
rubric.minimum_fix: Water entry increases turgor pressure, raising the cell's water potential until it equals the soil's, at which point net water movement stops.

items.stem: A researcher measures the water potential of a plant cell and finds it is more negative than the surrounding soil solution.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States unaffected carriers (Aa) pass the recessive allele without expressing it; two carrier parents can produce affected children (aa).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how an autosomal recessive disorder can skip generations in a pedigree.
rubric.minimum_fix: Carriers (Aa) do not express the disorder but can pass the allele; two carriers mating have a 1/4 chance of producing an affected (aa) child.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Mother is aa; father's father was aa so father is Aa with probability 1/2; probability of affected child = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
rubric.learner_facing_text: A woman with the disorder (aa) has children with a man whose father had the disorder. State the probability their first child is affected.
rubric.minimum_fix: The father is Aa with probability 1/2; probability of affected child = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

items.stem: A scientist analyzes a pedigree in which an autosomal recessive disorder appears in every other generation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States after meiosis I: 2 cells each with 2 chromosomes (still consisting of 2 chromatids each, n=2); after meiosis II: 4 cells with 1 chromosome each.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the chromosome arrangement at the end of meiosis I and meiosis II for a cell with 2n=4.
rubric.minimum_fix: After meiosis I, 2 cells each contain 2 chromosomes (2 chromatids each); after meiosis II, 4 cells each contain 1 single chromatid.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I) generate new allele combinations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain two ways meiosis generates genetic diversity.
rubric.minimum_fix: Crossing over exchanges alleles between homologs; independent assortment randomly orients homologous pairs, producing diverse gametes.

items.stem: During meiosis, a cell with four chromosomes (2n=4) undergoes both meiosis I and meiosis II.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States restriction enzymes recognize and cut specific palindromic sequences; the number and position of cut sites determines fragment sizes.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how restriction enzymes generate different-sized DNA fragments from a longer DNA molecule.
rubric.minimum_fix: Each restriction enzyme cuts at its specific palindrome; the distance between cut sites determines the size of each resulting fragment.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fragments are loaded into gel and an electric field pulls them through; smaller fragments move faster and farther; compared to ladder for size estimate.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates the DNA fragments and how size is determined.
rubric.minimum_fix: Electric current drives fragments through the gel; smaller fragments migrate farther in a given time; band position is compared to a size ladder.

items.stem: A student extracts DNA from human cheek cells and runs a gel electrophoresis after restriction enzyme digestion.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States: (1) denaturation — heat separates DNA strands; (2) annealing — primers bind to complementary sequences; (3) extension — DNA polymerase synthesizes new strand.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the three steps of a single PCR cycle and what happens in each.
rubric.minimum_fix: Denaturation (95°C) separates strands; annealing (~55°C) allows primers to bind; extension (72°C) has Taq polymerase extend from primers.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3'-OH; primers provide the starting 3'-OH end flanking the target sequence.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why primers are necessary for PCR.
rubric.minimum_fix: Primers provide a 3'-OH end for Taq polymerase to extend from; without primers, polymerase cannot initiate DNA synthesis.

items.stem: Researchers use PCR (polymerase chain reaction) to amplify a small region of ancient mammoth DNA.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States soil already exists with nutrients and seed banks; pioneer species do not need to build soil from scratch.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why secondary succession proceeds more rapidly than primary succession.
rubric.minimum_fix: Existing soil and buried seeds allow plants to establish quickly; no need to weather rock or build soil as in primary succession.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States early successional trees are sun-loving but their shade prevents their own seedlings from establishing; shade-tolerant species grow beneath and eventually replace them.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the role of shade tolerance in determining which tree species dominate the climax community.
rubric.minimum_fix: Early colonizing trees create shade; shade-tolerant climax species establish under their canopy and eventually outcompete sun-loving pioneers.

items.stem: A forest community experiences a fire that kills most trees but leaves intact soil and seed banks.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States higher temperature increases kinetic energy of water molecules; greater vapor pressure inside leaf vs. outside air increases transpiration rate.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why transpiration rate is higher at 35°C than at 20°C.
rubric.minimum_fix: At 35°C, water vapor pressure inside the leaf is higher relative to the air, increasing the gradient that drives water loss through stomata.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States guard cells take up K+ (and water follows by osmosis), becoming turgid and bowing open the stoma; losing K+ causes stomata to close.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how guard cells control transpiration by opening and closing stomata.
rubric.minimum_fix: Guard cells accumulate K+, water follows by osmosis, they become turgid and bow apart opening the stoma; K+ loss reverses this.

items.stem: A student investigates whether temperature affects the rate of transpiration in a plant by measuring water loss at 20°C and 35°C.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fossil fuels store carbon removed from the atmosphere long ago; burning them releases ancient CO2 faster than natural processes can remove it.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle.
rubric.minimum_fix: Combustion of fossil fuels converts long-sequestered organic carbon to CO2, rapidly adding carbon to the atmosphere beyond natural cycling rates.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States CO2 is a greenhouse gas; it absorbs outgoing infrared radiation and re-radiates it back to Earth's surface, raising temperature.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the increase in atmospheric CO2 affects global temperature.
rubric.minimum_fix: CO2 absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth and re-emits it back, trapping heat in the atmosphere and raising global temperatures.

items.stem: A biologist studies the carbon cycle and notes that burning fossil fuels releases CO2 that was sequestered millions of years ago.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States Rhizobium receives carbohydrates (energy) from the plant; the plant receives fixed nitrogen (NH3/NH4+) it could not otherwise use.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mutualistic relationship between Rhizobium and legumes in terms of what each partner gains.
rubric.minimum_fix: Rhizobium receives sugars from the plant for energy; the plant gains fixed nitrogen (NH4+) from Rhizobium, which plants cannot make.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States most organisms cannot use N2 directly; nitrogen fixation converts it to bioavailable forms (NH4+, NO3-) needed for amino acids and nucleotides.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why nitrogen fixation is important for ecosystems, given that N2 makes up 78% of the atmosphere.
rubric.minimum_fix: N2 is unusable by most organisms; fixation converts it to NH4+ that plants can absorb for building proteins and nucleic acids.

items.stem: Researchers find that a mutualistic relationship between nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) and legume plants increases soil nitrogen.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the change alters R group chemistry; interactions that maintain 3D shape are disrupted, changing the active site or binding surface.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a single amino acid change can cause a protein to lose its function.
rubric.minimum_fix: A different R group changes the chemical interactions holding the protein's shape; if the active site is altered, the protein cannot bind substrate.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States primary structure is directly altered (sequence changes); this ripples into tertiary and quaternary by disrupting folding interactions.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the level of protein structure most directly affected by changing one amino acid and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Primary structure is directly altered; since tertiary and quaternary structure depend on primary sequence, folding is disrupted throughout.

items.stem: A researcher studying protein structure finds that a single amino acid substitution causes a protein to misfold and lose function.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States somatic cells are body cells that are not passed to offspring; only mutations in gametes (egg or sperm) are heritable.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a somatic mutation cannot be passed to offspring.
rubric.minimum_fix: Somatic mutations affect only the individual's body cells; gametes are separate and do not carry the somatic mutation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States proto-oncogene mutation causes overactive growth signals (gas pedal stuck); tumor suppressor mutation removes the brake; both needed to bypass all controls.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how mutations in both a proto-oncogene and a tumor suppressor gene can cooperate to cause cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: A proto-oncogene mutation drives excess cell division (stuck gas pedal) while tumor suppressor loss removes the brake, together causing cancer.

items.stem: A student observes that a somatic cell mutation in skin cells causes one person's cells to divide uncontrollably but does not affect their offspring.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States vaccine contains weakened/killed pathogen or antigen; immune system responds, forming memory cells without causing illness.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a vaccine triggers immunity without causing disease.
rubric.minimum_fix: A vaccine presents antigens from the pathogen; the immune system produces antibodies and memory cells without the harmful effects of the real disease.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States memory B and T cells persist after primary exposure; upon re-exposure, they rapidly proliferate and produce antibodies/cytotoxic T cells.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the immune response to a second exposure to influenza is faster and stronger than the first.
rubric.minimum_fix: Memory cells created during the primary response proliferate quickly upon re-exposure, clearing the pathogen before symptoms develop.

items.stem: A researcher compares the immune response of a person vaccinated against influenza to one who has never been exposed.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the repressor binds the operator (DNA sequence near promoter), sterically blocking RNA polymerase progression.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism by which the repressor protein silences gene transcription.
rubric.minimum_fix: The repressor binds the operator, physically blocking RNA polymerase from moving along the template and silencing transcription.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States inducer binds repressor's allosteric site, changing its shape so it can no longer bind the operator; RNA polymerase can now transcribe.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the inducer molecule reverses repressor-mediated silencing.
rubric.minimum_fix: Inducer binding changes the repressor's conformation, reducing its affinity for the operator; the repressor falls off and transcription begins.

items.stem: Scientists sequence the promoter regions of an inducible gene and find a short palindromic sequence where a repressor protein binds.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fungal hyphae extend far beyond the root's reach into soil, dramatically increasing surface area for phosphorus absorption.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how mycorrhizal associations increase plant phosphorus uptake.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fungal hyphae extend into soil far beyond roots, increasing the surface area available to absorb phosphorus from soil particles.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States both partners benefit: plant gains phosphorus (and water); fungus gains carbohydrates; neither is harmed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why this association is considered mutualistic rather than parasitic.
rubric.minimum_fix: The plant receives phosphorus and the fungus receives sugars — both benefit from the relationship, defining it as mutualism.

items.stem: A tropical plant has adapted to very low phosphorus soils by forming associations with mycorrhizal fungi.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions are channels connecting adjacent cells; ions flow directly from one cell to the next, propagating the action potential.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how gap junctions allow electrical signals to spread between heart muscle cells.
rubric.minimum_fix: Gap junctions create direct cytoplasmic connections; ions (the electrical signal) flow through the channels into adjacent cells without crossing membranes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions fail; electrical signals cannot spread uniformly across the heart; uncoordinated contraction (arrhythmia) results.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to heart rhythm if connexin proteins were nonfunctional.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without functional gap junctions, electrical signals cannot coordinate across cells; contractions become uncoordinated, causing arrhythmia.

items.stem: A researcher disrupts the expression of a gene encoding a gap junction protein (connexin) in heart muscle cells.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States zooxanthellae perform photosynthesis inside coral tissue providing sugars; coral provides CO2, nutrients, and shelter.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mutualistic relationship between corals and zooxanthellae.
rubric.minimum_fix: Zooxanthellae produce sugars by photosynthesis that feed the coral; the coral provides CO2 and inorganic nutrients to the algae.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States bleached corals die, eliminating the structural habitat of the reef; many reef species depend on coral structure, reducing biodiversity.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why coral bleaching caused by rising ocean temperatures threatens the entire reef ecosystem.
rubric.minimum_fix: Dead bleached coral loses its structural complexity, eliminating habitat for the diverse fish and invertebrates that depend on it.

items.stem: A biologist studying coral reefs notes that as ocean temperatures rise, corals expel their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) and bleach.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States intermediate birth weights have highest survival; very low (underdeveloped) and very high (difficult delivery) weights have lower survival.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism of stabilizing selection using birth weight as an example.
rubric.minimum_fix: Intermediate birth weight maximizes infant survival; too low risks underdevelopment and too high risks delivery complications, both reducing fitness.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States stabilizing: mean unchanged, variance decreases; directional: mean shifts toward one extreme, variance may also change.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Contrast stabilizing selection with directional selection in terms of effect on mean phenotype and variation.
rubric.minimum_fix: Stabilizing selection maintains the mean but reduces variance; directional selection shifts the population mean toward one extreme.

items.stem: A scientist studies stabilizing selection in human birth weight, finding that very low and very high birth weights have higher infant mortality.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States founder effect = small group colonizes new area; bottleneck = existing population drastically reduced. Both reduce genetic diversity by chance.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the founder effect and how it differs from the bottleneck effect.
rubric.minimum_fix: The founder effect occurs when a small group establishes a new population; bottleneck reduces an existing population. Both reduce diversity by genetic drift.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States one consequence: low genetic diversity, higher frequency of alleles carried by founders, increased risk of inbreeding.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict one genetic consequence of the founder effect for the island finch population.
rubric.minimum_fix: The island population will have low genetic diversity; alleles that were rare in the mainland population may be common if founders happened to carry them.

items.stem: An island 1000 km from the mainland is colonized by a small group of finches blown off course during a storm.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States biological species concept = can interbreed and produce viable offspring; if these populations still interbreed they are one species.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain whether these moth populations represent two species using the biological species concept.
rubric.minimum_fix: Under the biological species concept, organisms that can interbreed and produce viable fertile offspring are one species; these populations qualify.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the river prevents migration between populations; without gene flow, each population accumulates different mutations and adaptations by selection and drift.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the river acts as a barrier to gene flow and could eventually lead to speciation.
rubric.minimum_fix: The river prevents individuals from crossing, stopping gene flow; each population diverges independently until reproductive barriers evolve.

items.stem: Researchers compare two populations of the same moth species separated by a river. They find the populations have diverged in wing pattern but can still interbreed.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States GPP = total energy fixed by photosynthesis; NPP = GPP minus autotroph respiration; only NPP energy is stored in biomass available to consumers.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the difference between GPP and NPP and why NPP is more relevant to consumers.
rubric.minimum_fix: GPP is total photosynthesis; autotrophs use some for their own respiration; NPP is what remains as biomass for consumers to eat.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States less light reduces photosynthesis rate; GPP falls and NPP falls; less energy available to support consumer populations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how a decrease in solar radiation (e.g., from sediment runoff) would affect NPP in the reef.
rubric.minimum_fix: Less solar radiation reduces the rate of photosynthesis, lowering GPP and NPP, reducing the energy available to support reef animals.
