items.stem: A coral reef ecosystem has high primary productivity. Researchers measure gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must list all five: large population (prevents drift), random mating (prevents assortative mating), no mutation, no migration, no selection.
rubric.learner_facing_text: State the five conditions required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and explain what each prevents.
rubric.minimum_fix: Large population prevents drift; random mating prevents unequal partner choice; no mutation, no migration, and no selection prevent allele frequency changes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States natural selection is occurring (differential survival); this violates the no natural selection condition.
rubric.learner_facing_text: A researcher finds that homozygous dominant individuals have higher survival rates. Explain which H-W condition is violated.
rubric.minimum_fix: Differential survival based on genotype means natural selection is acting, violating the no-selection condition of H-W equilibrium.

items.stem: A population geneticist finds that allele frequencies in a large, randomly mating beetle population do not change across generations.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States hemoglobin has 4 polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure); myoglobin has 1 polypeptide (tertiary structure).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the structural difference between hemoglobin and myoglobin.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hemoglobin has four subunits (quaternary structure); myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain with only tertiary structure.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States myoglobin does not show cooperativity and binds O2 tightly at low concentrations; hemoglobin releases O2 at low partial pressures to tissues.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why myoglobin has a higher O2 affinity than hemoglobin at low partial pressures of O2.
rubric.minimum_fix: Myoglobin binds O2 tightly at low concentrations for storage; hemoglobin's cooperativity causes it to unload O2 at the lower partial pressures found in tissues.

items.stem: A researcher compares the structure of hemoglobin in humans and myoglobin in muscle tissue.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue; without NAD+, glycolysis halts and ATP production stops.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the metabolic purpose of alcoholic fermentation in yeast.
rubric.minimum_fix: Yeast use fermentation to oxidize NADH back to NAD+, allowing glycolysis to keep running and producing 2 ATP per glucose.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States aerobic respiration uses pyruvate in the Krebs cycle and ETC to produce ~30 ATP; fermentation only yields 2 ATP from glycolysis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why alcoholic fermentation is less efficient than aerobic respiration.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fermentation only captures energy from glycolysis (2 ATP); aerobic respiration extracts additional energy from pyruvate via Krebs and ETC (~30 ATP total).

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates that when yeast are given glucose in the absence of oxygen, they produce ethanol and CO2 (alcoholic fermentation).

rubric.evidence_requirements: States an insertion shifts the entire reading frame of all codons downstream; a substitution only changes one codon (one amino acid).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a single nucleotide insertion is more disruptive than a single nucleotide substitution.
rubric.minimum_fix: An insertion alters the reading frame for all downstream codons, changing every amino acid after it; a substitution only affects one codon.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the ribosome terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that lacks its C-terminal domain and is likely nonfunctional.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a premature stop codon resulting from a frameshift mutation would affect the protein product.
rubric.minimum_fix: A premature stop codon terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that is missing C-terminal sequences and usually nonfunctional.

items.stem: A scientist introduces a frameshift mutation by inserting one nucleotide into the middle of a protein-coding gene.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transposase enzyme cuts the transposon from its location and inserts it into a new site (cut-and-paste); or copies itself and inserts the copy.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how a transposon moves from one location in the genome to another.
rubric.minimum_fix: Transposase cuts the transposon out of the DNA and ligates it into a new genomic location, or makes a copy that inserts elsewhere.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transposon insertion can disrupt a gene's coding sequence or regulatory region, inactivating or altering its expression.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how transposons can cause mutations when they insert into a new location.
rubric.minimum_fix: Inserting into a coding region disrupts the reading frame; inserting into a promoter may silence the gene by blocking RNA polymerase.

items.stem: A scientist discovers a bacterium that produces a toxin by means of a mobile genetic element that can jump between chromosomes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States: damage causes JA synthesis; JA travels to undamaged cells; binds receptors; activates transcription factors; defense genes expressed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the signal transduction pathway from herbivore damage to JA-induced gene expression in a plant.
rubric.minimum_fix: Wounding triggers JA synthesis; JA moves to distal cells, binds receptors, activates transcription factors, and induces protease inhibitor genes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States JA (or salicylic acid) is transported through phloem to undamaged leaves; those leaves pre-emptively activate defense genes.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how systemic acquired resistance allows undamaged parts of the plant to respond to herbivore damage.
rubric.minimum_fix: Systemic signals like JA travel through the phloem to undamaged leaves, which upregulate defense genes before the herbivore reaches them.

items.stem: A researcher studying plant defense responses finds that jasmonic acid (JA) is produced when a plant is damaged by herbivores.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States guide RNA contains a ~20-nucleotide sequence complementary to the target DNA; it base-pairs with the target strand, positioning Cas9 to cut.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how the guide RNA directs Cas9 to the correct genomic location.
rubric.minimum_fix: The guide RNA base-pairs with its complementary target DNA sequence, positioning Cas9 adjacent to the PAM site so it can cut both strands.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States tumor suppressor normally halts cell division in response to DNA damage or errors; without it, damaged cells proliferate unchecked.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why disabling the tumor suppressor gene caused tumors to develop in the mice.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without the tumor suppressor, cells with DNA damage or errors cannot be halted or directed to apoptosis, and they proliferate uncontrollably.

items.stem: A scientist uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disable a tumor suppressor gene in mice and observes the development of tumors.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States photosynthesis rate equals cellular respiration rate; CO2 fixed by photosynthesis equals CO2 released by respiration — no net gas exchange.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain what is happening at the light compensation point in terms of CO2 exchange.
rubric.minimum_fix: At the compensation point, the rate of CO2 fixation by photosynthesis equals the rate of CO2 release by respiration; net exchange is zero.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States plant cannot fix enough carbon to replace what respiration consumes; carbohydrate stores are depleted and the plant eventually dies.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what happens to carbohydrate stores in a plant kept below its light compensation point for an extended period.
rubric.minimum_fix: Below the compensation point, respiration exceeds photosynthesis; the plant consumes stored carbohydrates until reserves are depleted.

items.stem: A researcher measures the effect of light intensity on net photosynthesis rate. Below a threshold, the plant releases more CO2 than it fixes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States behavioral (prezygotic) isolation; female frogs recognize only conspecific calls and do not approach other species, preventing mating.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify the frog mating call as a type of reproductive isolating mechanism and explain how it prevents hybridization.
rubric.minimum_fix: The species-specific call is a behavioral prezygotic barrier; females only approach males whose call matches, preventing cross-species mating.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name one: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, or hybrid breakdown; explains correctly.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Give one example of a postzygotic isolating mechanism and explain how it reduces hybrid fitness.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hybrid sterility is postzygotic: mules (horse x donkey) are born healthy but cannot reproduce, reducing hybrid fitness to zero.

items.stem: Students studying animal behavior observe that male frogs produce species-specific calls, and females approach only males of their own species.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States natural selection is non-random (fit alleles increase); genetic drift is random chance; selection produces adaptation, drift does not.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how genetic drift differs from natural selection as a mechanism of evolution.
rubric.minimum_fix: Natural selection favors alleles that improve fitness in a non-random way; drift causes random changes regardless of whether an allele is beneficial.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States small samples show more sampling error; chance events change allele frequencies dramatically; large populations buffer these random events.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why genetic drift has a greater effect in small populations than in large populations.
rubric.minimum_fix: In small populations, a single chance event (like one individual failing to reproduce) changes allele frequencies dramatically; large populations buffer random variation.

items.stem: A class simulates evolution by randomly drawing colored beans (alleles) from a jar to model genetic drift in a small population.
